fields.Front: A data-extraction agent reads multi-page supplier contracts and fills a JSON record of line items. Its loop, written directly on the Claude API, gives Claude three tools (fetch_page, lookup_vendor and validate_totals) and runs exactly six iterations, then returns whatever fields have been filled. Contracts of up to four pages extract correctly. For longer contracts the records are missing the line items from later pages, and the logs show that the sixth response in those runs had a stop_reason of "tool_use" with a pending fetch_page call that was never executed. Which change to the loop best fixes the incomplete records? A. Raise the fixed count from six iterations to twelve, and return whatever fields have been filled when it is reached. B. Keep the six-iteration loop, and instruct the model in the system prompt to complete each contract within six tool calls. C. Continue while Claude requests a tool call, stop when Claude ends its turn, and keep a high limit as a safeguard. D. Stop the loop as soon as a response contains text that summarizes the fields extracted up to that point.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. When the loop exits, the last response has a stop_reason of "tool_use" and a pending fetch_page call, so Claude was not finished: the fixed count ended the task, not Claude. The loop should be driven by the stop reason, continuing on "tool_use" and terminating on "end_turn"; a high limit can remain as a guard against runaway loops, but not as the normal way to stop. Option A keeps an arbitrary cap as the stopping mechanism, so any contract that needs more than twelve calls is cut short the same way. Option B is a prompt-only fix that pressures Claude to skip pages to fit a budget, and any run that still needs more than six calls is cut off by the same cap. Option D swaps one anti-pattern for another, since a response can contain text and a tool call together. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.1 References: • How tool use works — The agentic loop (client tools) • Stop reasons and fallback — tool_use • How the agent loop works — Turns and messages

fields.Front: Your team wrote the tool loop for a returns-and-billing support agent directly against the Claude Messages API. After each response the loop inspects the content blocks: if any block is text, it sends that text to the customer and ends the turn. In testing, a customer asks where a replacement order is. The API response contains a text block reading "Let me pull up that order for you." followed by a tool_use block for lookup_order, and its stop_reason is "tool_use". The customer receives only the sentence about pulling up the order, and nothing more arrives. What is the root cause of the incomplete reply? A. The response was cut off at the output token limit before Claude could add the order status after the tool call. B. The loop treats the presence of assistant text as completion, although the stop reason shows Claude is waiting on a tool. C. The description of lookup_order is too vague, so Claude described its intention instead of actually calling the tool. D. The loop left the tool definitions out of the request, so Claude could only describe the lookup in a text block.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. The response has a stop_reason of "tool_use" and carries a tool_use block, so Claude has paused for the result of lookup_order; text that accompanies a tool call is a preamble, not a final answer. The loop should run the tool, append the assistant message and a tool_result, and call the API once more, ending only on "end_turn". Checking for assistant text as a completion signal is an anti-pattern the exam guide names. Option A is wrong because a truncated response reports "max_tokens", not "tool_use". Option C is wrong because Claude did request the tool: the block is in the response. Option D is wrong because a tool_use block for lookup_order shows that the tool definition reached Claude. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.1 References: • How tool use works — The agentic loop (client tools) • Handle tool calls — Handling results from client tools • Stop reasons and fallback — tool_use

fields.Front: Your team wrote the tool loop for a returns-and-billing support agent directly against the Claude Messages API. A customer writes, "I was charged twice, please fix it." The API response contains a single text block, "I can help with that. Could you tell me the order number or the email used for the purchase?", no tool_use block, and a stop_reason of "end_turn". A teammate argues that the turn is unfinished because no tool has run, and wants the loop to keep calling the API until Claude calls one of the support tools. What should the loop do with this response? A. Append a user message saying "Continue" and call the API until a response arrives that contains a tool_use block. B. Show the text to the customer and close the support case as resolved, with no further requests to the API. C. Treat the response as a failed turn and retry the same request with a higher max_tokens value. D. End the loop, show the text to the customer, and send a new request when the customer's reply arrives.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. A stop_reason of "end_turn" means Claude finished its turn, and here that turn is a clarifying question only the customer can answer, so the loop ends and returns the text; the conversation moves on when the customer's reply is appended as a new user message. A loop continues only while the stop reason is "tool_use". Option A invents a user turn the customer never sent and pushes Claude to act without the order number or email it has just asked for. Option B stops sending requests and closes the case, although Claude's question is unanswered and the double charge is still unfixed. Option C misreads the signal: a truncated response reports "max_tokens", and this one ended naturally with nothing cut off. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.1 References: • Stop reasons and fallback — end_turn • How tool use works — The agentic loop (client tools)

fields.Front: An engineer builds a codebase-exploration assistant that calls the Claude API directly, with two custom tools, search_code and read_file. To keep requests small, each iteration of the loop sends only the system prompt, the engineer's question, and a user message containing the output of the most recent tool call. Asked "Which services call the deprecated billing client, and what timeout does each one pass?", the assistant runs search_code, reads the first matching file, runs the identical search, reads the same file, and keeps cycling until the engineer stops it. Every tool call succeeds and returns correct output. What is the most likely root cause? A. Each request leaves out the earlier tool calls and their results, so Claude cannot see what it has already found. B. The loop has no iteration limit, so nothing forces the assistant to stop searching and give the engineer an answer. C. The two tool descriptions overlap, so Claude cannot tell when it should search and when it should read a file. D. The system prompt does not tell the assistant to avoid repeating a tool call that it has already made.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The Messages API is stateless, so Claude can reason only over what each request contains. Because the loop sends just the latest tool output, the search results are gone by the time the file contents arrive, and the file contents are gone when the search results come back, which produces the cycle. A correct loop appends every assistant response and every tool result to the conversation history, so each iteration sees all prior findings and can choose a new action. Option B would end the cycling without producing an answer, and makes an arbitrary cap the stopping mechanism. Option C is not supported by the transcript: Claude picks a sensible tool each time. Option D cannot work, because the calls it should avoid repeating are not visible to it. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.1 References: • How tool use works — The agentic loop (client tools) • Using the Messages API — Multiple conversational turns • Handle tool calls — Handling results from client tools

fields.Front:
A multi-agent research system built on the Claude Agent SDK has a coordinator and four subagents: web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report generation. The coordinator is set up to send every request through all four in sequence, and the product requires every answer to cite a retrieved source. A user asks, "What year did the General Data Protection Regulation take effect?" The system takes several minutes and returns a multi-section report in which one sentence answers the question. Users with broad research topics are satisfied with the same pipeline.

How should the coordinator handle a request like this one?

A. Run the full four-subagent pipeline as it does today, so that every answer has the same depth and format.
B. Keep the full pipeline for all requests, but lower each subagent's turn limit so that it finishes sooner.
C. Analyze what the request needs and invoke only the web search subagent, returning the short answer and its source.
D. Answer from the coordinator's own knowledge without invoking any subagent, and return the year with no source.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. The request is a single fact, so it needs one lookup and a source, not document analysis, multi-source synthesis or a formatted report. Part of a coordinator's role is deciding which subagents to invoke from the complexity of the query instead of routing everything through the full pipeline; here that means web search alone, which also meets the citation requirement. Option A keeps the behavior that produced minutes of waiting and a report nobody asked for, and uniform depth is no benefit when the question is narrow. Option B still runs four stages, three of them with no real work to do, and a lower turn limit risks cutting short the broad topics the pipeline handles well. Option D skips retrieval, so the answer carries no retrieved source, which the product requires. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.2 References: • Subagents in the SDK — Automatic invocation • Prompting best practices — Subagent orchestration

fields.Front:
A multi-agent research system built on the Claude Agent SDK has a coordinator and four subagents: web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report generation. The coordinator is set up to send every request to the web search subagent alone and to return what it finds, and the product requires every answer to cite a retrieved source. A user uploads six regulatory filings and asks for a comparison of how three jurisdictions regulate cross-border data transfers, covering enforcement trends and open disputes. The reply is a short answer drawn from two web pages; it ignores the filings and covers one jurisdiction.

How should the coordinator handle a request like this one?

A. Split the work by jurisdiction and source type across search and document analysis, then invoke synthesis and reporting.
B. Invoke only the web search subagent, as it does today, and return the short answer together with the sources it found.
C. Keep the single web search subagent, and raise its turn limit so that it has time to cover all three of the jurisdictions.
D. Ask the user to split the request into separate questions, one for each jurisdiction and one more for the six filings.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The request has several parts: three jurisdictions, six uploaded filings, enforcement trends and open disputes. It needs web search for current developments, document analysis for the filings, and synthesis and report generation to turn the findings into a comparison. A coordinator decides which subagents to invoke from what the query requires, and its role covers decomposition, delegation and aggregation of results. Option B is the behavior that produced a reply covering one jurisdiction and none of the filings. Option C leaves the filings unread, since a longer web search still does not analyze uploaded documents, and gives no stage the job of comparing jurisdictions. Option D hands the coordinator's decomposition work to the user and still yields separate answers with no comparison across jurisdictions. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.2 References: • Subagents in the SDK — Automatic invocation • Prompting best practices — Subagent orchestration

fields.Front:
For a report on grid-scale battery storage, a coordinator agent plans four subtopics: cost trends, safety incidents, supply chains and permitting rules. Its search subagents return rich material for the first three and two short sources for permitting rules. The synthesis subagent then produces a draft whose permitting section is two sentences long. The coordinator currently passes whatever synthesis returns straight to the report generation subagent, so the thin section reaches the user unchanged.

What should the coordinator do when a synthesis draft comes back like this?

A. Tell the synthesis subagent to expand any thin section of its draft using its general knowledge of the subject.
B. Evaluate the draft for gaps, re-delegate targeted permitting queries, then re-invoke synthesis on the new findings.
C. Re-invoke the synthesis subagent on the same findings, with an instruction to cover permitting rules in more depth.
D. Double the number of sources that every search subagent must return for every subtopic in every future run.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. The gap is specific and visible in the draft: one of four planned subtopics has almost no material. The coordinator is the component that holds the plan, so it should compare the synthesis output against that plan, send targeted permitting queries to the search and analysis subagents, and re-invoke synthesis with the added findings, repeating until coverage is sufficient. Option A fills the section with unsourced text, which a research report can neither attribute nor verify. Option C reruns synthesis on the same two short sources, so the section can only be padded, not better supported. Option D spends more on the three subtopics that were already well covered and, with no evaluation step, cannot tell whether the permitting gap has closed. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.2 References: • Prompting best practices — Research and information gathering • Create custom subagents — Chain subagents

fields.Front:
To speed up source gathering, the coordinator agent of a multi-agent research system spawns three web search subagents in parallel. Each one receives the identical prompt: the user's topic, "effects of remote work on urban economies", and an instruction to return ten strong sources. When the results come back, 22 of the 30 sources are duplicates, nearly all of them about office vacancy rates, and nothing covers transit revenue or local retail, both of which the user's request mentioned.

Which change to the coordinator's delegation addresses both the duplication and the missing coverage?

A. Remove the duplicate sources from the combined results before the coordinator passes them to the synthesis subagent.
B. Let the three subagents message one another during the search, so that each one can skip what another has found.
C. Replace the three subagents with a single search subagent that is asked to return thirty sources on the topic.
D. Assign each subagent a distinct subtopic or source type, such as office vacancy, transit revenue or local retail.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. All three subagents received the same prompt, so each ran the same obvious searches; identical instructions produce overlapping results and leave the less obvious parts of the topic untouched. Partitioning the scope, by giving each subagent a distinct subtopic or source type, removes the overlap where it starts and makes transit revenue and local retail someone's assignment. Option A cleans up after the fact: the list gets shorter, and coverage is still limited to office vacancy. Option B adds coordination among subagents that bypasses the coordinator, and avoiding repeats does not assign anyone the missing subtopics. Option C gives up the parallel speed-up and still leaves the choice of angles to one undirected prompt, so the same skew toward office vacancy is likely. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.2 References: • Create custom subagents — Run parallel research • Prompting best practices — Subagent orchestration

fields.Front:
In a multi-agent research system, a developer wanted to save tokens, so the web search subagent writes its results to a shared file and the document analysis subagent reads that file directly. The coordinator only starts the two subagents and receives a one-line status message from each. During one run a search timed out and the search subagent wrote nothing. The analysis subagent read a leftover file from an unrelated run, and the final report cited sources that had nothing to do with the topic. The coordinator's logs showed two successful subagent runs.

Which design change best prevents this class of failure?

A. Have each subagent return its results and errors to the coordinator, which decides what to pass to the next subagent.
B. Have the analysis subagent check the shared file's modification time and skip any file that looks out of date to it.
C. Instruct the search subagent in its prompt to always write a file, even when a search fails or reaches a timeout.
D. Give the analysis subagent the web search tools, so that it can gather its own sources whenever the file is missing.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The failure stayed invisible because results and errors moved between subagents without passing through the coordinator: the timeout never reached it, so it had no chance to retry the search or hold back the analysis step. In the hub-and-spoke design the exam guide describes, the coordinator handles all communication among subagents, which gives it observability, one consistent place for error handling, and control over what each subagent receives. Option B patches one symptom with a heuristic and still hides the search failure. Option C depends on a prompt instruction being followed during the very failure it is meant to cover. Option D merges two roles and leaves the coordinator unaware that a search failed. Currency note (Oct 2026): current Claude Code docs say named subagents can message each other, so routing through the coordinator is a design choice, not a platform limit. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.2 References: • Create custom subagents — Chain subagents • Extend Claude Code — Compare similar features

fields.Front: A research system on the Claude Agent SDK defines a document analysis subagent with an AgentDefinition that sets description and prompt and leaves tools unset. The subagent is meant to read only the reports and spreadsheets that a user uploads. In several runs it also ran web searches and mixed web content into its analysis, so the final report attributed claims to the uploaded documents although they came from web pages. The team wants this subagent to be unable to reach the web at all. Which change achieves that? A. Add a sentence to the subagent's prompt telling it to use only the uploaded files and never the web. B. Set tools in its AgentDefinition to the file-reading tools, since an omitted field inherits every tool. C. Rewrite the subagent's description so that it says the subagent analyzes uploaded documents only. D. Have the coordinator review the subagent's output and delete any claim that seems to come from a web page.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. In an AgentDefinition, tools is the field that restricts what a subagent can use. When it is omitted, the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents, which is how a document analyst ended up searching the web. Listing only the file-reading tools leaves the web tools out of its session, so the restriction no longer depends on what the model chooses to do. Option A is a prompt instruction: it lowers the rate of web use without making it impossible, and the team asked for impossible. Option C edits the field that tells the coordinator when to use this subagent, which has no effect on the tools the subagent holds. Option D acts after the fact and cannot be reliable, because the coordinator has no dependable way to tell which claims came from a web page. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.3 References: • Subagents in the SDK — AgentDefinition configuration • Subagents in the SDK — Tool restrictions

fields.Front: A team builds a research coordinator on the Claude Agent SDK. Three subagents (web search, document analysis and synthesis) are defined in code, each with a clear description, and the coordinator's system prompt tells it to delegate to them by name. In test runs the coordinator answers every question itself: the logs show its own searches and file reads, and no subagent invocation at all. The coordinator's allowedTools setting is ["WebSearch", "WebFetch", "Read"]. Which configuration change is needed for the coordinator to invoke its subagents? A. Add "Task" to the tool list of each of the three subagents, so that they can accept delegated work. B. Move the three subagent definitions out of code and into Markdown files under .claude/agents/. C. Add "Task" to the coordinator's allowedTools, since subagents are spawned through the Task tool. D. Enable fork_session on the coordinator, so that its three subagents can share its session history.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is the answer the exam expects. The exam guide states that subagents are spawned through the Task tool and that a coordinator's allowedTools must include "Task" for it to invoke them; this coordinator's list holds only search and file tools, which fits a coordinator that does all the work itself. Option A puts the tool on the wrong agents: the delegating agent is the one that calls it, and a subagent does not need it to receive work. Option B changes where the definitions live, and defining subagents in code is supported and is the recommended way for SDK applications. Option D misuses fork_session, which gives a resumed session a new session ID and plays no part in spawning subagents. Currency note (Oct 2026): current Agent SDK docs name this tool Agent and describe allowedTools as the tools to auto-approve, with unlisted tools still available, so by those docs a missing entry alone does not remove the tool. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.3 References: • Subagents in the SDK — Detect subagent invocation • Configure permissions — Allow and deny rules • Subagents in the SDK — Programmatic definition (recommended)

fields.Front:
A coordinator agent delegates to a web search subagent through the Task tool. At the start of the coordinator's conversation the user said that only sources published since 2022 are acceptable, and asked for a balanced view of regulatory, legal and industry perspectives. The coordinator's delegation prompt reads: "1. Search for 'offshore wind permitting delays'. 2. Open the first three results. 3. Summarize each in two sentences." The subagent returns three nearly identical summaries of one developer's press releases, two of them from 2019.

Which two changes to the delegation prompt best address these results? (Select TWO.)

A. Remind the subagent to apply the constraints that the user gave during the conversation with the coordinator.
B. Add further numbered steps, such as opening the first ten results and writing three sentences about each one.
C. Write the user's publication-date requirement into the prompt, since the subagent cannot see that conversation.
D. State the research goal and the quality criteria, and leave the choice of searches and sources to the subagent.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C and D. Options C and D are correct. The numbered procedure fixed one query and the first three results, so the subagent had no room to look for regulatory, legal and industry sources when the top results turned out to be one developer's press releases; a prompt that states the goal and the quality criteria lets it adapt its searches (Option D). The date requirement lived only in the coordinator's conversation, and a subagent receives nothing but the prompt it is given, so the requirement has to be written into that prompt (Option C). Option B adds procedure, which keeps the rigidity and returns more of the same skewed results. Option A refers the subagent to a conversation it has no access to, so there is nothing for it to apply. Currency note (Oct 2026): current Agent SDK docs name the Task tool the Agent tool. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.3 References: • Subagents in the SDK — What subagents inherit • Prompting best practices — Subagent orchestration

fields.Front: Logs from a research coordinator built on the Claude Agent SDK show a repeating pattern. The coordinator is covering four subtopics for a report on semiconductor supply chains (fabrication capacity, rare materials, export controls and logistics): it emits one Task tool call, waits for that subagent's result, and only in its following response emits the call for another subtopic. Each subagent takes about ninety seconds, so gathering takes about six minutes. No subtopic depends on the findings of the others. Which change most directly reduces the time spent gathering? A. Raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS so that the coordinator is allowed to run more subagents at once. B. Merge the four subtopics into one Task tool call, so that a single subagent covers all of them in one run. C. Have the coordinator emit all four Task tool calls in one response, so that the subagents run in parallel. D. Switch the four subagents to a smaller and faster model, so that each of them finishes its research sooner.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. The four subtopics are independent, and the delay comes from how the calls are issued: one Task tool call per response, each waiting for the one before it, so the total is the sum of four runs. When the coordinator emits all four Task tool calls in a single response, the subagents run concurrently and gathering takes about as long as the slowest one. Option A raises a ceiling that is not in play: the default already allows 20 subagents at once, and this coordinator never has more than one running because it waits for each result before issuing the next call. Option B hands all four subtopics to a single subagent, which works through them in sequence inside one context. Option D trades research quality for speed on each run and keeps the sequential pattern that causes most of the delay. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs name the Task tool the Agent tool, and say subagents run in the background by default unless Claude needs a result before continuing. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.3 References: • Subagents in the SDK — Benefits of using subagents • Create custom subagents — Run subagents in foreground or background • Prompting best practices — Optimize parallel tool calling

fields.Front:
A coordinator agent on the Claude Agent SDK has finished gathering material on microplastics in drinking water. Its own conversation holds the web search subagent's results and the document analysis subagent's summaries of twelve studies. It then invokes the synthesis subagent through the Task tool with the prompt "Synthesize the findings gathered so far into a two-page summary." The summary that comes back is fluent and generic: it mentions none of the twelve studies and contains figures that appear in no source the system retrieved.

What is the most effective fix?

A. Give the synthesis subagent the web search tools, so that it can look up the twelve studies for itself.
B. Add a line to the synthesis subagent's system prompt telling it to use only the findings gathered so far.
C. Resume the coordinator's session before each synthesis call, so that the subagent shares its history.
D. Include the complete search and document analysis outputs directly in the synthesis subagent's prompt.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. A subagent invoked through the Task tool starts with a fresh context. It does not see the coordinator's conversation, so the search results and study summaries held there never reached it, and "the findings gathered so far" pointed at nothing. The only channel from coordinator to subagent is the prompt of the call, so the complete outputs of the prior agents belong directly in that prompt. Option A makes the subagent repeat finished work and may surface different sources. Option B restricts the subagent to findings it does not have, so the instruction cannot supply the missing content. Option C changes nothing, because resuming the coordinator's session does not alter what a subagent receives. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs name the Task tool the Agent tool, and Claude Code also documents a fork type of subagent that inherits the whole conversation, while other subagents start fresh. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.3 References: • Subagents in the SDK — What subagents inherit • Create custom subagents — Fork the current conversation

fields.Front:
A coordinator agent on the Claude Agent SDK has finished gathering material on microplastics in drinking water. Its own conversation holds the web search subagent's results and the document analysis subagent's summaries of twelve studies. Before invoking the synthesis subagent, the coordinator rewrites all of this material into several paragraphs of continuous prose and includes the whole text in the subagent's prompt. The summary that comes back reflects the studies accurately, but its citations are unreliable: some claims have no source, and two statistics are attributed to the wrong paper and page.

What is the most effective fix?

A. Pass each finding as structured data that keeps the claim separate from its source URL, document name and page number.
B. Add an instruction to the synthesis subagent's prompt telling it to double-check every citation before it responds.
C. Ask the document analysis subagent to analyze all twelve studies a second time before synthesis is invoked.
D. Shorten the prose to a list of the main conclusions, so that the synthesis subagent has less text to keep track of.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The content reached the synthesis subagent, which is why the summary is accurate. What was lost is the link between each claim and its source: rewriting everything as continuous prose blended the findings with their URLs, document names and page numbers, or dropped them. Passing the findings in a structured format, with each claim in one field and its source metadata in others, lets the subagent carry attribution through unchanged. Option B asks the subagent to verify citations against information that is not in its context. Option C repeats work whose output was sound: the attribution was lost in the coordinator's rewrite, which a second analysis does not change. Option D removes more detail, including what attribution survived the rewrite. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.3 References: • Subagents in the SDK — What subagents inherit • Prompting best practices — Long context prompting

fields.Front: A customer support agent has the tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund and escalate_to_human. To enforce identity verification, a hook blocks process_refund unless get_customer has already been called in the conversation. An incident review finds a refund sent to the wrong account: get_customer had returned "status": "no_match" for a misspelled email address, the agent then issued the refund using an account number the customer typed into the chat, and the hook allowed the call. Which change closes this gap? A. Add a system prompt rule telling the agent to decline a refund when get_customer has found no match. B. Remove the hook and rely on few-shot examples that show a successful verification before each refund. C. Make the hook block process_refund outright and route refund requests to human agents through escalate_to_human. D. Have the hook require that get_customer has returned a verified customer ID, not merely that it was called.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. The hook checks that get_customer was called, but the purpose of the prerequisite is that the customer's identity has been verified. A call that returns no match satisfies the first condition and not the second, which is the gap the incident exposed. The gate should block process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID. Option A adds prompt guidance to a financial operation, where instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate. Option B removes the programmatic enforcement that exists and replaces it with examples the model may not follow. Option C closes the gap by taking away the agent's ability to issue any refund, including refunds for verified customers, and moves that whole workload to human agents. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.4 References: • Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks — Add context and block a tool • Hooks reference — PreToolUse decision control

fields.Front:
A customer writes to a support agent: "My replacement phone arrived with a cracked screen, I was charged twice for shipping on the same order, and the loyalty points for the order never appeared on my account." The agent verifies the customer, investigates the cracked screen, arranges a replacement, and closes its reply without mentioning the duplicate charge or the missing points. Transcripts show the same pattern across multi-issue messages: the first issue is resolved well and the others are dropped. The three issues involve the same customer and order, and none depends on the outcome of the others.

How should the agent's workflow handle messages like this?

A. Split the message into distinct items, investigate each in parallel using shared context, then send one unified resolution.
B. Split the message into distinct items, handle them one after the other, and send a separate reply as each one is resolved.
C. Split the message into distinct items, give each one to a subagent with a fresh context, and forward each subagent's reply.
D. Raise the agent's iteration limit, giving its loop room to reach the second and third issues before the reply is written.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The message contains three separate concerns, and the agent's failure is that it treats the message as one issue and stops after the first. Decomposing the request into distinct items makes each one an explicit unit of work. Because the items share one verified customer and one order and do not depend on each other, they can be investigated in parallel with that shared context and then combined into a single reply that covers all three. Option B would cover every issue, but it adds delay for issues that are independent and splits the answer across three replies. Option C runs the items at once but throws away what they share: each subagent starts without the verified customer and the order, so that work is repeated three times, and the customer still receives three separate replies. Option D misreads the failure: the agent was not cut off by a limit, it ended its reply by choice after the first issue, so a higher limit changes nothing. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.4 References: • How the agent loop works — Parallel tool execution • Prompting best practices — Subagent orchestration

fields.Front: An accounts-payable agent built on the Claude Agent SDK processes supplier invoices with four tools: extract_header, extract_line_items, validate_totals and post_to_ledger. The system prompt says that validate_totals must pass before an invoice is posted. An audit of 4,000 processed invoices finds 31 that were posted with no validate_totals call, and nine of those carried wrong totals into books that have since been closed. The finance team says that a single unvalidated posting is unacceptable. Which change should the team make? A. Move the validation rule to the top of the system prompt and mark it as critical, so that the agent gives it more weight. B. Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks post_to_ledger until validate_totals has passed for that invoice. C. Add few-shot examples to the prompt that show validate_totals being called before each post_to_ledger call. D. Run a nightly job that re-validates the posted invoices and reports any whose totals turn out to be wrong.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. Posting an unvalidated invoice has a financial cost that cannot be undone once the books close, and the team needs it never to happen. A system prompt instruction is guidance that the model follows most of the time: 31 skipped validations in 4,000 invoices is the non-zero failure rate that prompt-based ordering carries. A programmatic prerequisite takes the decision away from the model, because the call to post_to_ledger is blocked unless validate_totals has returned a pass for that invoice. Option A and Option C are stronger versions of the same prompt-based approach; they may lower the rate, but neither can bring it to zero. Option D finds bad postings after they have reached the ledger, which is the outcome the finance team wants to rule out. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.4 References: • Extend Claude Code — Compare similar features • Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks — Add context and block a tool

fields.Front: An accounts-payable agent built on the Claude Agent SDK processes supplier invoices with four tools: extract_header, extract_line_items, validate_totals and post_to_ledger. The finance team would like extract_header to run before extract_line_items, because the run logs are easier to read in that order. About one run in twenty calls the two tools the other way round. The extracted data is identical either way, nothing downstream depends on the order, and the team says an occasional exception is fine. Which change fits this request best? A. Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks extract_line_items until extract_header has returned for that invoice. B. Replace the agent with a fixed script that calls the four tools in one hard-coded order for every invoice it receives. C. State in the system prompt that extract_header should be called before extract_line_items, and include a short example. D. Add a system prompt rule telling the agent to restart the invoice whenever it notices the two tools ran out of order.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. The order of the two extraction calls is a readability preference: the data is identical either way, nothing downstream depends on it, and the team accepts an occasional exception. Prompt-based guidance with an example fits that case, because its small failure rate costs nothing here. Programmatic enforcement is for steps where compliance must be guaranteed, such as a check that has to pass before money moves. Option A would guarantee the order, but it adds code to maintain and blocked calls the agent must recover from, in order to prevent an outcome that harms no one. Option B gives up the agent's ability to adapt to unusual invoices for the sake of tidier logs. Option D asks the model to notice its own slip and redo the invoice, which pays twice for a run whose data was already correct and still depends on the model complying. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.4 References: • Extend Claude Code — Compare similar features • Best practices for Claude Code — Set up hooks

fields.Front: Human agents at a support center work in a ticketing tool that is separate from the AI support agent's platform, so they cannot open the agent's conversation transcripts. When a case needs a person, the agent calls escalate_to_human. Today the escalation carries one line written by the agent, for example "Customer upset about a refund, please assist." Human agents then ask customers to repeat their account details and describe the problem a second time, and in several cases they issued a full refund on top of a partial refund the agent had already processed. Which two additions to the handoff would most directly fix these problems? (Select TWO.) A. A sentiment score for the conversation, so that human agents can see how upset the customer has become. B. The customer ID together with the root cause that the agent identified while it investigated the case. C. A link to the full conversation transcript, stored in the console of the platform that runs the agent. D. The refund amount and status already processed by the agent, together with the action it recommends.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B and D. Options B and D are correct. The human agents cannot see the transcript, so the handoff has to carry everything they need to act. The customer ID and the root cause the agent identified remove the need to ask the customer for account details and for the whole story a second time (Option B). The refund amount and status already processed, with a recommended action, tell the human agent what has been done and what remains, which prevents a second refund on top of the first (Option D). Option A describes the customer's mood, which identifies neither the account nor the problem nor the work already completed. Option C points to a transcript that the human agents cannot open from their ticketing tool, and reading a whole transcript is slower than reading a summary of it. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.4 References: • Customer support agent — Establish success criteria • Customer support agent — Integrate Claude into your support workflow

fields.Front: A support agent built on the Claude Agent SDK has a hook that intercepts process_refund calls and denies any refund above $500. The hook returns the denial with no explanation. Transcripts show what happens after a denial: the agent retries process_refund with the same amount two or three times, then tells the customer there is a "technical problem" and ends the conversation. None of these customers reaches a human agent, although an escalate_to_human tool is available and the policy is that refunds above $500 go to a human for approval. Which change to the hook fixes this behavior? A. Have the hook rewrite the refund amount to $500 with updatedInput and allow the amended call to go through. B. Remove the hook, and state the $500 rule and the escalate_to_human path in the system prompt. C. Return a reason with the denial that states the approval rule and tells the agent to call escalate_to_human. D. Let the call through, and have a PostToolUse hook notify a supervisor after each refund above $500.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. The hook enforces the limit, but it gives the agent nothing to act on, so the agent treats the denial as a passing failure, retries, and then gives up. A denial can carry a reason that is shown to the model; when that reason states the rule and names the alternative, the agent stops retrying and calls escalate_to_human, which is the redirect to human approval that the policy asks for. Option A uses updatedInput to change what the customer receives: the policy calls for approval of the requested refund, not for a silent reduction to $500. Option B gives up guaranteed enforcement and returns to an instruction the model follows only most of the time. Option D lets the refund through first, and a PostToolUse hook fires only after the tool has already executed, so the approval the policy requires never happens. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.5 References: • Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks — Add context and block a tool • Hooks reference — PreToolUse decision control • How the agent loop works — Tool permissions

fields.Front: A customer support agent built on the Claude Agent SDK uses MCP tools owned by three backend teams. The orders tool returns timestamps as Unix epoch seconds, the billing tool returns ISO 8601 strings, and the shipping tool returns numeric status codes such as 3 for "delivered". The system prompt explains all three formats, yet in about 4% of conversations the agent misjudges whether an order is inside the 30-day return window or misreads a shipment's status. The backend teams will not change their output formats. Which change addresses the errors most reliably? A. Add more worked examples of each timestamp format and each status code to the agent's system prompt. B. Add a hook that intercepts the agent's outgoing tool calls and blocks any call to a tool with a nonstandard format. C. Have the agent call each tool twice and compare the two results before it relies on a date or a status. D. Add a PostToolUse hook that converts timestamps and status codes to one format before the model sees them.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. The data is right, and the misreadings happen when the model interprets three different formats; the prompt already explains them, and a 4% error rate is what probabilistic compliance looks like. A PostToolUse hook runs after each tool completes and can replace the tool's output before the model sees it, so every timestamp and status code reaches the model in one consistent form on every call, whatever the model would have made of the raw value. Option A is more of the approach that already leaves a residual error rate. Option B acts on the wrong side of the tool: the problem is in the results coming back, and blocking the calls would deprive the agent of data it needs. Option C returns the same formats twice, so there is nothing new to compare. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.5 References: • Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks — Outputs • Hooks reference — PostToolUse decision control

fields.Front: A customer support agent built on the Claude Agent SDK uses MCP tools owned by three backend teams, including process_refund and escalate_to_human. Company policy requires human approval for any refund above $500, and the system prompt states the limit. A quarterly review finds that 14 of 6,200 refunds were above $500 and were issued with no approval. The finance team wants that number to be zero, and wants customers who ask for larger refunds to be handed to a human agent. Which change meets both requirements? A. Add a hook that blocks process_refund calls above $500 before they run and directs the agent to escalate_to_human. B. Add a PostToolUse hook on process_refund that alerts the finance team every time a refund above $500 has been issued. C. Restate the $500 limit in the system prompt with several examples of refund requests being escalated to a human. D. Add a PostToolUse hook that rewrites the result of any refund above $500 to say that approval is required.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. The requirement is zero refunds above $500 without approval, and 14 exceptions in 6,200 show that the limit stated in the prompt is followed only most of the time. A hook that intercepts the outgoing process_refund call, a PreToolUse hook in the Agent SDK, runs before the tool does. It can block any call above the limit regardless of what the model decided, and its response can direct the agent to escalate_to_human, which meets the second requirement. Option B and Option D both use PostToolUse, which fires after the tool has completed: by then the refund has been issued, and an alert or a rewritten result changes only what people or the model see afterwards. Option C strengthens the prompt, which may reduce the 14 but cannot guarantee zero. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.5 References: • Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks — Add context and block a tool • Hooks reference — PreToolUse • Hooks reference — PostToolUse decision control

fields.Front: A structured data extraction agent built on the Claude Agent SDK assembles shipment records as JSON. It gathers fields through MCP tools from two servers: the customs server always returns dates as DD/MM/YYYY, and the carrier server always returns ISO 8601 dates. The output is requested with a JSON schema whose date fields must be ISO 8601 strings, and every record passes schema validation. An audit nevertheless finds records in which a customs date such as 03/04/2025 was written as 2025-03-04, with the day and month swapped. Which change addresses the root cause? A. Add a PostToolUse hook that converts the customs server's dates to ISO 8601 before the model processes the results. B. Tighten the JSON schema so that every date field must match a strict ISO 8601 pattern for year, month and day. C. Add a retry loop that re-runs the extraction with the validation error whenever a record fails the schema validation. D. Add few-shot examples to the system prompt that show a customs date being converted with the day placed first.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. Each server's format is fixed and known, so converting customs dates to ISO 8601 is a mechanical rule; the errors arise because that conversion is left to the model, which sometimes reads 03/04 as March 4. A PostToolUse hook can replace a tool's output before the model sees it, so every customs date arrives in the target format and there is nothing left to misread. Option B cannot catch the error, because the swapped value 2025-03-04 is itself a well-formed ISO 8601 date. Option C never fires, since every affected record passes schema validation; a schema checks structure, not whether a value is the right one. Option D improves the odds, but an example is followed only most of the time, and the audit needs the conversion to be right on every record. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.5 References: • Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks — Outputs • Hooks reference — PostToolUse

fields.Front: The customer experience team has a request for a support agent built on the Claude Agent SDK, which already uses a hook to block refunds above its approval limit. When a customer is eligible for both a refund and store credit, the team would like the agent to mention store credit first, because it is processed faster. The customer still chooses freely, both outcomes are within policy, and the team says it is fine if the agent sometimes leads with the refund when that suits the conversation. How should this request be implemented? A. Add a hook that blocks process_refund unless the transcript shows that store credit was offered first. B. Add the preference to the system prompt, with an example reply that mentions store credit before a refund. C. Add a PostToolUse hook that removes the refund option from eligibility results, so that only store credit appears. D. Route eligible customers through a classifier to a second agent that is able to offer store credit only.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. The request is a preference about wording and order: both outcomes are within policy, the customer chooses, and the team accepts occasional deviation. That is the case for prompt-based guidance, whose compliance is probabilistic, and an example reply makes the preference concrete. Hooks earn their cost when a business rule needs guaranteed compliance, like the refund limit this agent already enforces. Option A turns a preference into a hard gate, so refunds the policy allows would be blocked whenever the agent led with the refund, which the team said is fine. Option C hides the refund option from the model, so customers would lose a choice they are entitled to. Option D removes the same choice and adds a classifier and a second agent to maintain. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.5 References: • Extend Claude Code — Compare similar features • Automate workflows with hooks — How hooks work

fields.Front:
You are using an agent built on the Claude Agent SDK to add tests to a legacy billing service that nobody on the current team wrote. The repository has about 400 source files, no architecture document, and almost no existing tests. A first attempt used a fixed pipeline that walked the directories alphabetically and wrote tests one file at a time. It spent most of its budget on trivial utility modules, and many generated tests failed because they did not account for shared database fixtures or for a pricing module that most other modules depend on.

Which decomposition approach fits this task best?

A. Keep the fixed per-file pipeline, and run it in parallel across several subagents so that the repository is covered sooner.
B. Map the structure, identify high-impact areas, then follow a prioritized plan that is revised as dependencies emerge.
C. Give the agent the whole repository in one prompt and ask it for a complete test suite in a single pass.
D. Keep the fixed pipeline, but reorder it so that the largest files in the repository are tested before the others.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. The task is open-ended: the structure, the important modules and their dependencies are unknown at the start, which is what the first attempt ran into with the shared fixtures and the pricing module. For this kind of work the exam guide calls for dynamic decomposition: map the structure, identify high-impact areas, then build a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered. Fixed pipelines suit predictable, repeatable work such as a multi-aspect review. Option A makes the same unprioritized pipeline faster without changing what it works on or in what order. Option C asks one pass to hold 400 files and leaves no room to adjust to findings. Option D fixes the order in advance too, and file size is not a measure of impact. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Explore first, then plan, then code • Prompting best practices — Chain complex prompts

fields.Front: A CI job runs Claude Code on every pull request. Because single-pass reviews of large pull requests gave uneven depth, the team already reviews each changed file in its own pass, and the per-file feedback has become consistent and detailed. A recent pull request changed the return type of parse_amount() in one file from a number to an object and left three callers in other files unchanged. Each per-file review reported no problems, because every file was internally consistent, and the mismatch reached production. Which change to the review design would catch this kind of defect while keeping the depth of the per-file reviews? A. Go back to a single pass over the changed files together, with each caller and its callee in the same context. B. Keep the per-file passes, and tell each one to flag every function whose signature other files might rely on. C. Keep the per-file passes, and attach the whole repository to each one as additional context for its review. D. Keep the per-file passes, and add a separate integration pass that examines data flow and interfaces across files.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. The per-file passes are doing their job for local issues; the bug that escaped is a cross-file one, a changed return type and callers that expect the old one, which no existing pass is positioned to see. The decomposition the exam guide describes has two parts: analyze each file individually, then run a separate integration pass focused on cross-file data flow. Option A restores the single pass whose uneven depth the team already moved away from. Option B asks each pass to guess about callers it cannot see, which flags most functions and verifies none of them. Option C re-creates attention dilution in every pass and gives no pass the specific job of checking interfaces between files. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.6 References: • Prompting best practices — Chain complex prompts • Best practices for Claude Code

fields.Front: A developer has spent an hour in a Claude Code session in which Claude analyzed a legacy payments module: its call graph, its side effects and its untested branches. She wants to compare two ways of making the module safe to refactor, characterization tests versus contract tests at the module boundary. Each approach should be explored in its own conversation that starts from the full analysis, the two explorations should not see each other's work, and the analysis session itself should stay as it is so that she can come back to it. Which approach fits these requirements? A. Use fork_session twice on the analysis session, and explore one testing approach in each of the two new forks. B. Resume the analysis session with --resume in two terminals, and explore one testing approach in each terminal. C. Explore the two approaches in turn in the analysis session, running /compact between them to keep them apart. D. Start two new sessions in separate git worktrees with --worktree, and repeat the analysis in each before exploring.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. Forking creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original's history and has its own session ID, while the original stays unchanged. Two forks therefore give two conversations that both begin from the full analysis, cannot see each other's work, and leave the analysis session intact, which matches all three requirements. Option B does not branch anything: --resume reopens the same session under the same ID, so two terminals write both conversations into one transcript, where their messages interleave. Option C keeps both explorations in one session: /compact only summarizes the conversation so far, so the second exploration begins from a summary that includes the first one's work rather than from the full analysis, and the analysis session itself is changed. Option D gives each exploration its own working copy but no analysis: neither new session holds it, so Claude must repeat the hour of work in each, and the two repeats can produce different baselines. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs spell this option fork_session in the Python SDK, forkSession in the TypeScript SDK, and --fork-session or /branch in the Claude Code CLI. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.7 References: • Manage sessions — Branch a session • How Claude Code works — Resume or fork sessions

fields.Front: A developer-productivity tool built on the Claude Agent SDK runs a long codebase analysis and stores the session ID when it finishes. A user then asks for two alternative refactoring proposals, one that extracts a shared library and one that keeps the code in place behind an adapter. Each proposal should be developed with the complete analysis in context, the two should have separate histories, and the stored analysis session should remain usable as the starting point for future requests. How should the tool run the two proposals? A. Spawn two subagents with the Agent tool from a new session, giving each a one-line description of its proposal. B. Run two queries with continue_conversation enabled and no session ID, one for each of the two proposals. C. Run two queries with resume set to the stored session ID and fork_session enabled, one for each proposal. D. Run one query with resume set to the stored session ID that develops the two proposals one after the other in it.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Resuming a stored session ID with fork_session enabled creates a new session that starts with a copy of the analysis session's history; the fork gets its own session ID, and the original's history stays unchanged. Doing this once per proposal gives two isolated branches that both hold the complete analysis, and the stored session remains a clean starting point. Option A fails the first requirement, because a subagent spawned this way starts with a fresh context and a one-line description carries none of the analysis. Option B continues the most recent session both times, and continuing picks up an existing session and adds to it, so the second proposal is developed on top of the first and the stored baseline is altered. Option D develops the second proposal with the first in context and also writes both into the stored session. Currency note (Oct 2026): fork_session is the Python SDK spelling, and current docs use forkSession in the TypeScript SDK and --fork-session or /branch in the Claude Code CLI. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.7 References: • Work with sessions — Fork to explore alternatives • Work with sessions — Continue, resume, and fork • Subagents in the SDK — What subagents inherit

fields.Front: A developer runs two long investigations with Claude Code in the same repository. On Monday she worked in a session she had named checkout-latency, in which Claude traced slow requests through four services. On Tuesday she started a separate session named flaky-tests in the same directory and worked in it until the evening. On Wednesday morning the code is unchanged, and she wants to carry on the latency investigation with everything Claude had already traced in context. Which command does that? A. Run claude --continue from the repository directory to pick the investigation back up. B. Run claude --resume checkout-latency from the repository directory to reopen that session. C. Run claude -n checkout-latency from the repository directory to open the session by name. D. Run claude --resume flaky-tests --fork-session to branch a copy for the latency work.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. She named the Monday session, and claude --resume followed by a session name resumes that specific conversation, with its full history of what Claude traced. The code has not changed, so that context is still valid. Option A reopens the most recent conversation in the current directory, which is the Tuesday session, flaky-tests. Option C uses the flag that sets a display name when a session is started, so it begins a new conversation and does not reopen the history of Monday's session. Option D resumes the wrong session and forks it: the copy would hold the flaky-test history and none of the latency analysis she wants to build on. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.7 References: • Manage sessions — Resume a session • Manage sessions — Name your sessions • CLI reference — CLI flags

fields.Front: A week ago a developer used a Claude Code session named billing-audit to analyze about forty files of a billing module, and the session ended with a set of refactoring recommendations. Since then one small pull request has merged. It changed two of those files, invoice_totals.py and tax_rules.py, and touched nothing else in the module. The developer wants Claude to turn the recommendations into an implementation plan that is correct for the code as it stands. What is the most effective way to proceed? A. Resume the session and ask for the implementation plan straight away, relying on the analysis already in its history. B. Start a new session and have Claude explore all forty files a second time before it writes the implementation plan. C. Resume the session and tell Claude which two files changed, so that it re-reads those and updates its analysis. D. Start a new session, paste in the old recommendations without mentioning the pull request, and ask for the plan.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Most of the session's context is still valid: thirty-eight of the forty files are unchanged, and the recommendations rest on that analysis. Resuming keeps it, but the history holds the contents of invoice_totals.py and tax_rules.py as they were a week ago, so Claude should be told that those two files changed and asked to re-read them before it plans. Option A lets Claude plan from the stale reads in its history, so the plan may contradict the merged pull request. Option B discards a valid analysis and pays for a full re-exploration when two files need a second look. Option D loses the detailed analysis behind the recommendations and hides the one fact Claude needs in order to check them. Currency note (Oct 2026): current Claude Code docs list a note that Claude Code adds on its own when a file Claude read earlier changes on disk, and naming the changed files yourself does not depend on it. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.7 References: • Manage sessions — What a resumed session restores • How Claude Code works — Context Claude Code adds on its own

fields.Front: A week ago a developer used a Claude Code session named billing-audit to analyze about forty files of a billing module, and the session ended with a set of refactoring recommendations. Since then a large restructuring has merged: most of those files were split, renamed or rewritten, and the session's history is full of file contents that no longer exist in that form. The developer believes only the high-level conclusions still hold, namely three business rules and the modules that own them, and wants an implementation plan that is correct for the code as it stands. What is the most effective way to proceed? A. Resume the session and give Claude a list of every file that was split, renamed or rewritten since the analysis ran. B. Resume the session and ask for the implementation plan straight away, relying on the analysis in its history. C. Fork the session with fork_session, so that the new branch leaves the outdated tool results behind. D. Start a new session with a structured summary of the conclusions that hold, and have Claude read the current code.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. Resuming restores the full history, including week-old tool results, and here most of those results describe files that have since been split, renamed or rewritten. A context dominated by stale file contents is an unreliable base, because Claude may reason from code that is gone. A new session given a structured summary of what holds, the three business rules and their owning modules, keeps the valuable conclusions and reads the current code with nothing outdated in context. Option A suits a case where a few files changed; here it means re-reading nearly everything on top of the stale history. Option B plans directly from outdated contents. Option C does not help, because a fork starts with a copy of the original's history, stale results included. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs spell the fork option fork_session in the Python SDK, forkSession in the TypeScript SDK, and --fork-session or /branch in the Claude Code CLI. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.7 References: • Manage sessions — What a resumed session restores • Work with sessions — Resume across hosts • Best practices for Claude Code — Manage context aggressively

fields.Front: A multi-agent research system has a document analysis subagent with two tools: analyze_content, which takes the raw text of a fetched web page, and analyze_document, which takes the ID of a PDF in the team's library. Each description runs to several sentences and states when to use that tool rather than the other. In a test harness with a one-line system prompt, the subagent picks the right tool on all 60 evaluation tasks. In production, tasks such as "pull the key figures from this web report on battery recycling" go to analyze_document, which fails because the page has no library ID. The production system prompt includes the line "When a task mentions a report, paper or study, call analyze_document." What is the most likely cause of the misrouting? A. The two tool descriptions overlap too much for the subagent to tell fetched web pages apart from library PDFs. B. A system prompt instruction keyed to words like "report" creates a tool association that overrides the descriptions. C. The coordinator's task text leaves out the source type that the subagent would need for choosing between the two tools. D. The input schema of analyze_document is loose enough to accept raw web text where a library ID is required.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. The descriptions are doing their job: with a one-line system prompt the subagent chose correctly on all 60 evaluation tasks. What production adds is the line that ties the words report, paper and study to analyze_document, so a task about a web report triggers that tool even though its description says it takes library PDFs. Option B is right: keyword-sensitive wording in a system prompt can create a tool association that overrides well-written descriptions, and the fix is to remove or reword that line. Option A names a real cause of misrouting, but these descriptions are detailed, state the boundary and work in testing. Option C is contradicted by the example task, which says the source is a web report. Option D concerns what the tool accepts after it has been chosen; a stricter schema would change the failure, not the selection. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1 References: • Prompting best practices — Tool usage • Define tools — Best practices for tool definitions

fields.Front: A multi-agent research system has a document analysis subagent with two tools. analyze_content is meant for the raw text of a fetched web page, and its description reads "Analyzes content and returns key information." analyze_document is meant for a PDF in the team's library, and its description reads "Analyzes a document and returns key information." Each tool takes a single free-text input. The subagent's system prompt describes its role and says nothing about which tool to use. In about a third of tasks the subagent sends a web page to analyze_document or a library PDF to analyze_content. Which change is the most effective fix for the misrouting? A. Add a system prompt rule that routes any task containing the words "web" or "page" to analyze_content. B. Tighten both input schemas so that each tool returns an error when it receives the wrong kind of source. C. Place a classifier call ahead of the subagent that labels each task and exposes only the matching tool. D. Rename analyze_content to extract_web_results and rewrite both descriptions to say when to use each.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Nothing but the tool definitions tells the subagent which tool fits: the system prompt is silent on tool choice, and the two names and one-line descriptions are nearly identical, so selection comes close to a coin toss. Option D removes the overlap at its source: it renames analyze_content to extract_web_results and gives each tool a description that says when to use it rather than the other. Option A patches the symptom with a keyword rule; it leaves the definitions ambiguous and misfires on tasks that lack those words or use them about a PDF. Option B acts after the wrong tool has been chosen, so each misroute costs a failed call instead of being prevented. Option C adds a model call and a component to maintain before the direct, low-cost fix has been tried. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1 References: • Define tools — Best practices for tool definitions • Give Claude custom tools — Create a custom tool

fields.Front: A structured data extraction system gives Claude one generic MCP tool, process_document, that takes the document text and a free-form instructions string. Depending on the instructions it returns a prose summary, a list of field values, or a yes/no judgment on whether a claim is supported by the source, always as unstructured text. A downstream JSON schema validator rejects about one result in five because it cannot tell which of the three shapes it has received, and Claude sometimes asks for a summary at a stage where field values are needed. Which change best addresses both problems? A. Split it into extract_data_points, summarize_content and verify_claim_against_source, each with defined inputs and outputs. B. Expand the process_document description with example instructions strings for each of the three result shapes it returns. C. Split it into process_contract, process_invoice and process_report, each keeping the free-form instructions string. D. Add a second model call that labels the shape of each process_document result before the validator runs on it.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Both symptoms come from one tool doing three jobs with no contract: Claude has to steer it through free-form instructions, and the validator receives text whose shape depends on what was asked. Option A splits it into extract_data_points, summarize_content and verify_claim_against_source, which turns the choice of operation into a choice of tool and lets each tool define its own inputs and outputs, so the validator knows what it will receive. Option B may improve the instructions Claude writes, but the result remains unstructured text of unknown shape. Option C splits along the wrong line: tools per document type would each keep the free-form instructions and all three result shapes, so both problems remain. Option D guesses the shape after the fact, adding a model call and a new source of error while doing nothing about wrong requests. Currency note (Oct 2026): current tool-use docs also advise consolidating closely related operations into one tool with an action parameter, so splitting fits operations with different outputs, as here. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.1 References: • Define tools — Best practices for tool definitions • Tools (MCP specification) — Output schema • Understanding MCP servers — How tools work

fields.Front: A customer support resolution agent looks up orders through a custom MCP tool, lookup_order. The tool's handler wraps its database query in a try/except block that returns an empty list whenever the query raises an exception. During a database slowdown that lasted two hours, queries timed out, and the agent told dozens of customers who had active orders, "I can't find any orders on your account." Several of them placed duplicate orders. On a normal day the same reply is correct for customers who have never ordered. What is the root cause of the incorrect replies? A. The tool's handler reports a query that failed in the same form as a query that matched no orders. B. The agent's system prompt lets it answer after one order lookup instead of confirming with a second. C. The tool's description states the result format too loosely for the agent to read an empty list. D. The database's query timeout is too short for busy periods and turns slow queries into failures.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is the root cause: the handler turns every exception into an empty list, so a query that timed out and a query that validly matched nothing look identical to the agent. It did what a correct empty result calls for and told customers they had no orders. An access failure needs a retry decision and should come back as an error (isError: true, with a transient category); an empty list should mean only that the query succeeded and found no matches. Option B implies a second lookup, which would have returned the same empty list during the slowdown. Option C blames the description, but the agent read the empty list correctly; the result itself was wrong. Option D names the trigger, not the cause: a longer timeout would mean fewer failed queries, yet each one that did fail would be reported as an account with no orders. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.2 References: • Give Claude custom tools — Handle errors • Tools (MCP specification) — Error handling

fields.Front: A customer support resolution agent looks up orders through a custom MCP tool, lookup_order. When the database query completes and matches no rows, the tool's handler returns a result with isError: true and the text "Lookup failed: no orders found." For customers who have just signed up and have never ordered, the agent calls lookup_order three or four times, apologizes for "a system problem" and escalates the conversation to a human. The database is healthy throughout, and each of those queries ran to completion. Which change to the tool is most appropriate? A. Mark the error result with isRetryable: true, so that the agent knows it may repeat the lookup. B. Add a counter to the handler that blocks a fourth identical lookup_order call within any single conversation. C. Tell the agent in the system prompt to treat any failed lookup as an account that has no orders. D. Return a successful result with an empty order list, and keep isError: true for failures such as timeouts.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. The queries succeeded: the database was healthy and each query ran to completion, finding no orders because these customers have never placed one. Reporting that outcome with isError: true tells the agent that the call failed, so it retries and then blames a system problem. Option D corrects the signal: a valid empty result is returned as a success with an empty list, and isError: true is kept for access failures such as timeouts, where a retry decision is needed. Option A makes matters worse by inviting retries of a query that will return the same nothing. Option B caps the wasted calls but leaves the agent believing that the lookup failed. Option C stops the retries by making every real failure read as an empty account, which misinforms customers during an outage. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.2 References: • Give Claude custom tools — Handle errors • Tools (MCP specification) — Error handling

fields.Front: A customer support resolution agent issues refunds through a custom MCP tool, process_refund. On about 4% of calls the payment processor answers with a 503 "service unavailable" before it has processed anything, and the same request succeeds when it is sent a few seconds later. The tool reports every failure in one way: a result with isError: true and the text "Refund could not be completed." When this happens the agent tells the customer that the refund is not possible and escalates the case to a human, although the customer was eligible and nothing was wrong with the request. Which change to the tool's error result best fixes this behavior? A. Return isError: false with an empty result in place of the current generic error result. B. Keep isError: true and append the handler's full stack trace to the existing error text. C. Add an errorCategory of transient, isRetryable: true and a short description of the failure. D. Add an errorCategory of permission, isRetryable: false and an apology to pass on to the customer.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. The failure is temporary: the processor returned a 503 before processing anything, and the same request succeeds seconds later. The agent cannot learn that from "Refund could not be completed", which reads exactly like a refusal. The structured metadata in option C — an errorCategory of transient, isRetryable: true and a readable description — tells the agent that a retry is the right recovery, so eligible customers get their refund without escalation.
