Option A hides the failure behind a success, so the agent may tell the customer that the refund went through. Option B shows where the code failed, not whether another attempt would help. Option D mislabels a temporary outage as a permission failure that cannot be retried, which keeps the needless escalations. errorCategory and isRetryable are a convention the tool author adopts inside the result; the MCP specification itself defines only the isError flag for marking a failure. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.2 References: • Tools (MCP specification) — Error handling • Give Claude custom tools — Handle errors • Handle tool calls — Handling errors with is_error

fields.Front: A customer support resolution agent issues refunds through a custom MCP tool, process_refund. Company policy allows a refund only within 30 days of delivery, and the backend rejects any request outside that window. The tool reports every failure in one way: a result with isError: true and the text "Refund could not be completed." For a customer whose order was delivered 47 days ago, the agent calls process_refund three more times with the same arguments, then tells the customer that "a technical problem" is preventing the refund. Which TWO additions to the tool's error result would correct this behavior? (Select TWO.) A. An errorCategory of transient, so that the agent waits briefly before it resends the request. B. A retriable: false flag, so that the agent stops resubmitting a request that cannot succeed. C. The backend's internal rule ID and stack trace, so that the agent can work out what was rejected. D. A customer-friendly explanation of the 30-day limit, so that the agent can tell the customer why.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B and D. The rejection is a business rule, not a fault: the order was delivered 47 days ago and policy allows refunds only within 30 days, so no retry can succeed. Two things are missing from the generic error. A retriable: false flag (B) tells the agent to stop resubmitting, and a customer-friendly explanation of the 30-day limit (D) gives it something accurate to say in place of "a technical problem". Option A mislabels a policy violation as a temporary fault and would invite more retries. Option C exposes internal details that neither stop the retries nor give the agent wording fit for a customer. The retriable flag and the explanation are a convention the tool author adopts inside the result; the MCP specification itself defines only the isError flag for marking a failure. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.2 References: • Tools (MCP specification) — Error handling • Give Claude custom tools — Handle errors

fields.Front: In a multi-agent research system, a coordinator gives a document analysis subagent a batch of twelve papers to summarize. The subagent loads each paper through an MCP tool on the team's document store. By the team's own convention, the tool's error results carry isError: true together with an errorCategory, an isRetryable flag and a description. On the fifth paper the tool returns errorCategory: "transient", isRetryable: true and the description "Store busy, retry in 2 seconds." The other papers load normally, and the subagent keeps access to the tool for the rest of its run. How should the subagent handle the failure on the fifth paper? A. Stop the batch and return a structured error to the coordinator, so that it can decide whether to retry. B. Retry the load inside the subagent after the short delay, and report upward only if it keeps failing. C. Skip the fifth paper and return the other eleven summaries to the coordinator as the complete batch. D. Return an empty summary for the fifth paper, so that the coordinator receives twelve results as expected.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. The tool has said how to recover: the error is categorized as transient, marked isRetryable: true and comes with a two-second wait, and the subagent keeps the tool. Option B is right because a subagent should resolve a transient failure like this locally by retrying, and pass a failure up only when it cannot be resolved, together with partial results and what was attempted. Option A hands the coordinator a decision that the error metadata has already answered, and stalls the other papers for a fault that clears in seconds. Option C silently drops a paper and misreports the batch as complete. Option D disguises a failed load as a valid empty result, so the coordinator cannot tell that anything is missing. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.2 References: • Give Claude custom tools — Handle errors • Tools (MCP specification) — Error handling

fields.Front: A coordinator in a multi-agent research system hands a document analysis subagent twelve papers to summarize, and the subagent loads each one through an MCP tool on the team's document store. Under a convention the team adopted, every error result from the tool has isError: true plus an errorCategory, an isRetryable flag and a description. For three of the papers the tool returns errorCategory: "permission", isRetryable: false and the description "Restricted collection: this service account has no read access." The other nine papers load and are summarized. The subagent has no tool that can change access rights. What should the subagent return to the coordinator? A. A failure for the whole batch, with the nine finished summaries discarded so that the run can be repeated. B. The nine summaries, after it has retried the three restricted papers several times with increasing delays. C. The nine summaries, plus a structured error that names the three papers, the permission failure and what it tried. D. The nine summaries, presented as the finished analysis because the restricted papers could not be read anyway.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. The three failures cannot be fixed where they occurred: the tool marks them as permission errors with isRetryable: false, and the subagent has no tool that changes access. That is the case for passing the problem up, and option C sends what the coordinator needs to decide: the nine completed summaries, which papers failed, the failure category and what was attempted. The coordinator can then seek access, substitute sources or have the gap noted in the report. Option A throws away valid work, and a repeat run would meet the same restriction. Option B wastes attempts on an error the tool has declared non-retryable. Option D hides the gap, so the final report would rest on nine papers while appearing to cover twelve. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.2 References: • Subagents in the SDK — Benefits of using subagents • Give Claude custom tools — Handle errors • Tools (MCP specification) — Error handling

fields.Front: A developer productivity agent built with the Claude Agent SDK helps engineers understand a legacy billing system. It was given a generic fetch_url tool so that it could read design documents on the internal wiki. Traces show that it also follows links found in code comments and README files: vendor blog posts, package registry pages and, twice, an internal admin endpoint. The fetched pages crowd its context with unrelated text, and the security team wants the agent's network access limited to wiki documents. Which change best meets both concerns? A. Keep fetch_url and add a system prompt rule that the agent may fetch only internal wiki documents. B. Replace fetch_url with a load_document tool that validates each URL as a wiki document before fetching it. C. Keep fetch_url and add a second tool that the agent should call first to check whether a URL is allowed. D. Remove fetch_url and ask engineers to paste the text of each design document into the conversation.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. The agent needs one narrow capability, reading wiki design documents, but holds a general one, and it uses the extra reach. Option B replaces fetch_url with a load_document tool that validates the URL before fetching, which makes the limit part of the tool: off-wiki links and the admin endpoint are refused in code, and the agent keeps the documents it needs. Option A is a prompt rule where the security team needs a guarantee; nothing stops the agent from fetching any URL. Option C leaves the unrestricted tool in place and depends on the agent choosing to call the checker first. Option D does remove the risk, but it also removes the capability and hands the work back to engineers, which defeats the purpose of the agent. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3 References: • Tools (MCP specification) — Security considerations • Give Claude custom tools — Create a custom tool

fields.Front: A structured data extraction pipeline calls the Claude API with three tools: extract_metadata, which returns a document's title, author and date, and two enrichment tools, lookup_author and classify_topic, which need those fields as inputs. The requests use the default tool_choice, and the system prompt says to extract metadata first. In about one run in ten, Claude's first call is lookup_author with an author name it has guessed from the opening lines. Extraction has to come before enrichment on every document, and enrichment may then use whichever tools fit. Which configuration guarantees the required first step? A. Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} on each request in the conversation, starting with the first. B. Keep the default tool_choice and reword the system prompt to state that extraction is mandatory before the enrichment tools. C. Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} on each request in the conversation. D. Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} on the first request, then enrich in follow-up turns.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. The requirement is a guarantee about one specific tool, and the scenario shows that a prompt instruction falls short of it: one run in ten starts with lookup_author. Option D uses forced tool selection naming extract_metadata on the first request, which makes that call certain; later requests return to the default so that Claude can choose among the enrichment tools. Option A guarantees only that some tool is called, and lookup_author would satisfy it. Option B is the approach that is already failing; stronger wording lowers the rate without making it zero. Option C forces extraction on every turn, so the enrichment tools are never called. Currency note (Oct 2026): current API docs say the newest Claude models reject any and named-tool tool_choice with a 400 error and recommend auto with strict tool use or structured outputs. fields.Front: A structured data extraction pipeline calls the Claude API with three tools: extract_metadata, lookup_author and classify_topic. Each input is a short note from an editor that needs exactly one of the three operations, and Claude is expected to pick which one. The requests use the default tool_choice, and the system prompt says to respond only with a tool call. In about one run in ten, Claude replies with a paragraph of text that describes what it would do and calls no tool. The downstream code reads only tool_use blocks and drops everything else, so each of those notes is lost. Which configuration should the team use? A. Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"}, so that Claude must call a tool but picks which of the three. B. Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}, so that a tool call is always present. C. Keep {"type": "auto"} and have the downstream code parse the intended operation out of the text reply. D. Keep {"type": "auto"} and resend each request until the response contains a tool_use block.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Two facts decide this: a tool call must be present every time, and Claude must stay free to choose among the three operations. Option A, tool_choice of {"type": "any"}, does exactly that: Claude has to call one of the provided tools, and no particular tool is imposed. Under the default auto, Claude may answer in text, which is the one-in-ten failure. Option B also guarantees a call, but always to extract_metadata, which is wrong for notes that need another operation. Option C builds a brittle text parser around the failure. Option D pays for repeated requests without guaranteeing a call. Forcing a call does not make its inputs schema-valid; strict tool use adds that. Currency note (Oct 2026): current API docs say the newest Claude models reject any and named-tool tool_choice with a 400 error and recommend auto with strict tool use or structured outputs. Domain 2 (Tool Design & MCP Integration) · Task 2.3 References: • Define tools — Forcing tool use • Errors — Forced tool use not supported • Strict tool use

fields.Front: A multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK has a coordinator and four subagents for web search, document analysis, synthesis and report writing. To keep the configuration simple, every subagent was given the same 18 tools, including web search and page fetching. Transcripts show the synthesis subagent running its own web searches halfway through a synthesis and mixing pages that no one has vetted into its findings, and at times calling fetch_page where format_citation was the tool it needed. Which change is the most effective way to address both problems? A. Add a line to the synthesis subagent's prompt telling it not to search the web or fetch pages itself. B. Move the synthesis subagent to a more capable model that can choose reliably among all 18 tools. C. Limit each subagent to the few tools its role needs, which removes search and fetch from synthesis. D. Insert a classifier ahead of each subagent turn that exposes only the one tool it predicts is needed.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Both problems trace to the shared set of 18 tools. With tools outside its specialization available, the synthesis subagent uses them, and with that many to choose from its selection becomes less reliable, as the fetch_page mix-up shows. Option C fixes both at once by restricting each subagent to the handful of tools its role needs; in the Agent SDK this is the tools list in each subagent definition, and a tool left out is absent from that subagent's session. Option A asks rather than prevents, and does nothing about the size of the tool set. Option B spends more on a model while keeping the cause. Option D adds a model call per turn and a new point of failure where a static list per role is enough. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs put the degradation at more than 30-50 loaded tools and offer tool search for large tool sets. fields.Front: A team that uses Claude Code wants it to work with Jira: read an issue's description and acceptance criteria, search issues, add comments and move issues between statuses. These are standard Jira operations, and a maintained community MCP server already provides all of them. An engineer proposes spending two sprints on an in-house Jira MCP server "so that we control every tool." The team has no Jira workflow of its own beyond these operations, and it has a backlog of product work waiting. Which approach should the team take? A. Build the in-house server, because full control over every tool justifies the two sprints for any integration. B. Skip MCP and have Claude Code call the Jira REST API with curl commands through the Bash tool. C. Adopt the existing community server, and keep custom servers for workflows that are specific to the team. D. Export all Jira issues to Markdown files in the repository each night and let Claude Code read those.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. What the team needs is standard — reading, searching, commenting on and transitioning issues — and a maintained community server already covers it, so building the same thing would cost two sprints for no added capability. Option C is right: adopt the existing server and keep custom servers for workflows that are specific to the team, which this team does not have. Option A treats control as a goal in itself and trades a backlog of product work for it. Option B gives up typed, described tools for hand-assembled requests and ad hoc credential handling. Option D supplies stale, read-only copies and cannot comment on an issue or change its status. Adopting a community server does call for one check: the docs advise verifying that you trust a server before connecting it. fields.Front: A developer productivity agent built with the Claude Agent SDK has the built-in Read, Grep and Glob tools and a code-index MCP server. The server's find_references tool resolves a symbol across the whole monorepo, including re-exports and renamed imports, and returns the file, line and enclosing function of each use. Its description reads only "Finds references." Asked where a function is used, the agent almost always runs Grep on the function's name and misses call sites that import it under an alias, although find_references would have listed them. What is the most effective first step to fix this? A. Remove Grep from the agent's allowed tools and leave find_references as its tool for searching code content. B. Add a system prompt section that explains how the monorepo re-exports functions and renames them on import. C. Add a routing step that calls find_references itself before the agent sees a request about usage. D. Expand the find_references description to say what it resolves, what it returns and when to use it over Grep.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. The agent picks tools from their descriptions, and "Finds references." gives it no reason to prefer the MCP tool over a built-in it already understands. Nothing says that find_references follows re-exports and renamed imports or returns file, line and enclosing function. Option D supplies that: a description of what the tool resolves, what it returns and when to use it over text search fixes the cause at low cost. Option A removes a tool the agent needs for error messages, strings and other content searches. Option B teaches the agent about aliasing but not about the tool, so it would chase aliases with extra Grep calls while the tool that resolves them stays unexplained. Option C builds routing infrastructure before the simple fix has been tried, and bypasses the agent's judgment on every usage request. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs say MCP tool search is on by default and loads only tool names and server instructions at session start, so they also advise server authors to write clear server instructions. fields.Front: Six developers share a repository and use Claude Code on it. The team lead has set up a GitHub MCP server that runs as a local process, but its entry sits in the lead's own ~/.claude.json, with the lead's personal access token written into the entry's env block. The other five developers do not see the server in their sessions. Each developer already exports a personal token as GITHUB_TOKEN in their shell. The team wants the server defined once, shared through version control, and no token committed to the repository. Which TWO changes together meet these requirements? (Select TWO.) A. Define the server in a .mcp.json file at the project root and commit that file to the repository. B. Have each developer copy the lead's entry, token included, into their own ~/.claude.json file. C. Set the token value in the server's env block to ${GITHUB_TOKEN} so each machine supplies its own. D. Describe the server and its start command in CLAUDE.md so that Claude Code launches it on request.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and C. The requirements are a single shared definition under version control and no committed secret. Project scope provides the first (A): a server defined in .mcp.json at the project root is checked in and reaches everyone who clones the repository. Environment variable expansion provides the second (C): with ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in the env block, each developer's own exported token is filled in when the server starts, so the file holds no credential. Option B shares the lead's personal token, keeps six copies that drift apart and puts nothing under version control. Option D confuses instructions with configuration; CLAUDE.md gives Claude guidance and is not where MCP servers are registered. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs describe three scopes — local (the default) and user, both stored in ~/.claude.json, and project in .mcp.json — and say Claude Code asks for approval before using project-scoped servers. fields.Front: Six developers share a repository and use Claude Code on it. The team's standard MCP servers are defined in a committed .mcp.json file at the project root. One developer wants to spend a week trying an experimental profiling MCP server that is unstable and that nobody else on the team uses. A colleague suggests adding it to .mcp.json "so that it is version-controlled like the others." The developer wants the server available in their own sessions without changing what teammates see. Where should the developer configure the experimental server? A. In the developer's own ~/.claude.json, where it stays personal and out of teammates' sessions. B. In the committed .mcp.json, with a README note asking teammates to decline its approval prompt. C. In the committed .mcp.json, with its command set through a ${VAR} that only this developer defines. D. In a second .mcp.json in the home directory, which Claude Code merges into every project.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. The decisive facts are that the server is experimental and used by one developer, and that teammates' sessions must not change. Option A fits: an entry in the developer's own ~/.claude.json is private to that account and is never committed, so nobody else is affected. Option B commits the entry and puts an approval prompt for an unstable server in front of every teammate. Option C also commits it; teammates get an entry that cannot start, along with a missing-variable warning. Option D describes a mechanism the docs do not provide: .mcp.json is read from the project root, and personal servers belong in ~/.claude.json. fields.Front: A developer asks Claude Code to change one entry in fixtures/slots.json, a test fixture that holds an array of 60 slot objects. Every object is byte-for-byte identical: {"state": "free", "owner": null}. The 17th slot has to become "held", and the other 59 must stay as they are. Claude's Edit call fails because the text it supplied as the anchor occurs many times in the file. Widening the anchor to include the neighbouring lines does not help, since those lines are identical as well and the longer text also matches more than once. What should Claude do to make the change reliably? A. Set replace_all: true on the Edit call and reuse the anchor text that matched many times in the file. B. Call Write on the same file path with the corrected 17th object as the content to be saved. C. Pass a regular expression to Edit as the anchor, written to match the 17th occurrence of the object. D. Read the whole file, then use Write to save the complete contents with the 17th slot changed.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Edit needs anchor text that occurs exactly once, and the scenario rules that out: all 60 objects are identical, and adding neighbouring lines produces text that also matches more than once. Option D is the reliable fallback: Read the full file, then use Write to save the complete contents with only the 17th slot changed, since Write replaces the whole file with what it is given. Option A does succeed as a call, but it changes all 60 slots. Option B misreads Write, which overwrites the file with the content provided and does not append or merge, so the fixture would shrink to one object. Option C assumes a feature Edit lacks; it performs exact string replacement, with no regex. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs list a longer old_string or replace_all: true as the remedies for a repeated match and do not describe the Read-then-Write fallback. fields.Front: An engineer who has just joined a team asks a developer productivity agent how a password reset email gets sent in a legacy codebase of several thousand files. The agent has the built-in Read, Grep and Glob tools and has not seen the repository before. The repository holds three services and a shared library, with no architecture documentation, and nobody on the team can say which module owns the feature. The engineer does know that the reset link in the email contains the path /reset-password. Which exploration approach should the agent take? A. Grep for /reset-password to find an entry point, Read that handler, then follow its imports one file at a time. B. Glob for every source file in the repository, then Read each match so that the whole picture is in context. C. Glob for file names that contain the word password, then answer from the list of paths it returns. D. Read the top-level README and package manifests, then infer the flow from the names of the modules.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. The agent has one concrete lead, the string /reset-password, and a repository far too large to read. Option A turns that lead into an entry point with Grep; reading the handler and then the files it imports traces the real flow while loading only the files that matter. Option B reads thousands of files up front, which fills the context window with unrelated code before any question is answered. Option C searches file names, and a list of paths that contain password shows neither which file handles the reset nor how the email is sent. Option D infers behavior from names without reading the code that implements it, which invites a confident wrong answer in a legacy system. fields.Front: A CI pipeline runs Claude Code to review each pull request in a TypeScript monorepo of about 4,000 files. One pull request changes the signature of a function named calculateShippingCost, adding a required region argument. To check that no caller was missed, the review job has to find every place in the repository where the function is called. The callers sit in checkout, invoicing and reporting modules, in files whose names have nothing to do with shipping. Which built-in tool use finds the callers most directly? A. Glob with the pattern **/*shipping*, to list the files whose names suggest that they deal with shipping costs. B. Grep for calculateShippingCost across the repository, to list the files and lines that contain the name. C. Glob with the pattern **/*.ts, followed by a Read of every file that the pattern returns from the repository. D. Read on each module's entry file, followed by a Read of every file that those entry files import.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. The task is a search of file contents: every line that calls calculateShippingCost, wherever it lives. Option B is right because Grep searches inside files for a pattern, so one search for the function name returns the callers in checkout, invoicing and reporting even though their file names say nothing about shipping. Option A searches paths, not contents, and the scenario says the callers' file names are unrelated to shipping. Option C would reach the callers only by reading every TypeScript file into context, which is slow and crowds out the review itself. Option D follows imports outward from the entry files, which costs many reads and can miss a caller. Read on each directory under src, to list the entries and pick out the test files by name.

Option C is right because Glob matches file paths against a pattern, and **/*.test.tsx matches every file with that suffix in any directory, which is exactly the team's convention. Option A searches contents and returns any file that contains describe(, including tests that are not component tests, while missing a test file written without it. Option B also searches contents: it finds files that mention the suffix in their text, such as configuration, not the files that carry it in their names. fields.Front: Three packages share one monorepo: a React storefront in packages/web, a billing API in packages/api and a reporting job in packages/etl. Name the docs/standards/ directory in each package's CLAUDE.md and tell Claude to consult it whenever relevant. D. Have each package's CLAUDE.md reference only the standards files that apply to it, using @ import syntax.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: the standards already exist as separate files and each package needs a different subset, so each package's CLAUDE.md can pull in just the files its maintainers choose with @path imports. Imported files are expanded into context alongside the file that references them, and the documents stay the single source of truth. Option A loads all five documents into every session, including standards irrelevant to the package at hand, and creates a second copy to maintain. Option B is the stale-copy problem the team wants to avoid. Option C is not an import: a path mentioned in prose loads nothing, so Claude sees a standard only if it decides to open the file. fields.Front: A payments team uses Claude Code on a shared repository. Whenever the tech lead works on the code, Claude wraps each database call in the team's retry helper and writes tests in the team's table-driven style. A new engineer clones the repository, starts Claude Code in it and gets code that follows neither convention. The repository contains no CLAUDE.md; the tech lead wrote both conventions into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on their own laptop when the project began. fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: the conventions live in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, a user-level file that applies only to the tech lead and is not shared with teammates through version control, so a fresh clone carries none of them. Moving them into a project-level CLAUDE.md, at the repository root or in .claude/, and committing it gives every teammate the same instructions. Option B does reach the new engineer, but through hand-copied personal files that drift apart and must be redone for every hire. Option C edits a file the new engineer's sessions never load. fields.Front: A payments team uses Claude Code on a shared repository whose project-level CLAUDE.md holds the team's coding conventions. fields.Front: In a design-system team's monorepo, every Storybook story file's name ends in .stories.tsx, and most sit next to the components they document, for example packages/checkout/src/Cart.stories.tsx and apps/admin/widgets/Table.stories.tsx. Enter plan mode and have Claude map the date-handling paths in the service before it proposes the change. B. Use direct execution, giving Claude the bug description, the function name and the failing test to confirm the fix. C. Delegate a survey of the service's timezone handling to the Explore subagent and review its summary first. D. Use direct execution, and have Claude also replace the service's date-parsing code with a timezone-aware library.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: the change is a single conditional in one function, the stack trace pins down the location, the engineer already knows the fix and a failing test will confirm it. The exam guide describes direct execution as appropriate for simple, well-scoped changes of this kind, such as a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace. Option A spends a planning pass on a change whose scope is already settled; plan mode earns its overhead on large, multi-file or architectural work. Option C launches a service-wide survey that the task does not need. Option D picks the right mode but widens a one-conditional fix into a library migration across the service, which adds risk and review effort to a hotfix whose scope is already settled. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.4 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Explore first, then plan, then code • Choose a permission mode — Analyze before you edit with plan mode

fields.Front:
A logistics team's shipment-tracking service depends on a date-handling library that has been deprecated. Forty-seven files import it, spread across the API layer, the batch jobs and the reporting module, and several of them rely on the library's undocumented lenient parsing. There are at least two workable routes: replace every call site with the standard library directly, or introduce a thin adapter first and migrate modules behind it. An engineer proposes telling Claude Code to start replacing imports file by file, since each edit looks mechanical.

How should the team approach the migration with Claude Code?

A. Follow the proposal with direct execution, relying on the tests to reveal any call sites that behave differently.
B. Use direct execution but begin with the reporting module, since it is the least critical place to learn the pitfalls.
C. Begin in plan mode so that Claude explores the usages and settles the migration approach before any file is changed.
D. Split the forty-seven files evenly across separate sessions so that each one handles a small, mechanical batch.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: forty-seven files across three areas, hidden reliance on lenient parsing and two workable routes make this a large, multi-file change with an architectural decision still open, which is what plan mode is for. Claude can explore the usages and propose an approach before any file is edited, so the team does not discover a wrong choice halfway through. Option A commits to the direct-replacement route without weighing the adapter and leaves behavior differences to be found late, when rework is costly. Option B is still unplanned execution; changing the starting point does not settle the approach. Option D parallelizes the edits before the design question is answered and scatters the context needed to keep the files consistent. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.4 References: • Choose a permission mode — Analyze before you edit with plan mode • Best practices for Claude Code — Explore first, then plan, then code • Common workflows — Plan before editing

fields.Front:
Fifty-two call sites of a home-grown HTTP client are due to be replaced with the vendor's SDK. An engineer spent a Claude Code session on the migration in plan mode: Claude mapped every call site, flagged six that depend on the old client's retry behavior and proposed a phased approach, which the engineer has reviewed, edited and is satisfied with. No file has been changed so far. A teammate recommends staying in plan mode for the remainder of the work "to keep the migration safe", asking Claude to carry out each phase from there.

What should the engineer do?

A. Stay in plan mode as the teammate suggests and ask Claude to apply each phase's edits from within that mode.
B. Discard the plan and restart with direct execution from a fresh prompt that simply names the vendor's SDK.
C. Approve the plan and switch to direct execution so that Claude implements the planned phases in order.
D. Keep refining the plan in plan mode until it lists the exact replacement text for all fifty-two call sites.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: the investigation is finished and the engineer is satisfied with the plan, so what remains is implementation. The exam guide pairs plan mode for investigation with direct execution for implementation, for example planning a library migration and then executing the planned approach. Approving the plan exits plan mode so that Claude can start editing. Option A cannot deliver the migration: in plan mode Claude researches and proposes changes without making them, so no phase would be applied. Option B throws away the mapping of call sites and the flagged retry cases that make the migration safe. Option D keeps planning after the approach is settled; fifty-two exact replacements are implementation detail that execution, checked against the plan, will produce anyway. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.4 References: • Choose a permission mode — Review and approve a plan • Best practices for Claude Code — Explore first, then plan, then code

fields.Front:
A developer has been asked to put a cache in front of a slow pricing service so that product pages load faster. They have never built a caching layer. They can state the goal, faster page loads without ever showing customers a wrong price, but when a colleague asks how stale a price may be, what should happen when the cache store is unreachable, or how a price change should evict entries, they have no answers and had not thought of the questions. They are about to start the work in Claude Code.

What is the most effective way to begin?

A. Write the complete test suite for the cache first and iterate on the failures that Claude's code produces.
B. Give Claude two or three example requests with the cached responses the service should return for them.
C. Have Claude implement a simple cache with default settings and adjust it as problems appear in production.
D. Ask Claude to interview the developer about invalidation, staleness and failure modes before implementing.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: the developer is working in an unfamiliar domain and, as the colleague's questions showed, does not yet know which decisions exist. The interview pattern has Claude ask questions that surface considerations the developer has not anticipated, such as cache invalidation strategies and failure modes, before any implementation. Option A requires the developer to specify expected behavior in tests, which they cannot do while the staleness and failure requirements are undecided. Option B has the same gap: examples communicate a transformation the developer already understands. Option C postpones the design questions until customers see wrong prices, the one outcome the goal rules out. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.5 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Let Claude interview you

fields.Front:
Product titles in an online catalog need to become URL slugs, and a developer has asked Claude Code for a function to do it. The developer has described the rules in prose twice, at increasing length: lowercase everything, use hyphens for spaces, strip punctuation, and handle accents and ampersands sensibly. Each generated version treats the unclear cases differently: one drops accented letters, another transliterates them, and a third turns an ampersand into "and" while the others delete it. The developer knows exactly which slug each title should produce.

What is the most effective next step?

A. Write a third, longer prose description that spells out each rule for accents and ampersands in full.
B. Ask Claude to interview the developer about the slug requirements before it writes another version.
C. Provide two or three concrete title-to-slug pairs that show the expected output for the unclear cases.
D. Enter plan mode so that Claude can compare slug-generation approaches and propose an architecture.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: two prose descriptions have already been interpreted inconsistently, and the developer knows the exact output wanted, so concrete input/output examples are the most effective way to pin the transformation down. Two or three title-to-slug pairs covering an accented letter and an ampersand show the expected result without leaving room for interpretation. Option A repeats the technique that has failed twice; more prose invites more readings. Option B suits a developer who has not worked out the requirements, whereas this one already knows every answer. Option D addresses design and scope, not an ambiguous specification of one small function. Currency note (Oct 2026): the platform prompting guide suggests three to five examples for few-shot prompts in general; the exam guide's wording for this technique is 2-3. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.5 References: • Prompting best practices — Use examples effectively • Best practices for Claude Code — Give Claude a way to verify its work

fields.Front:
Before asking Claude Code to build a CSV order-import module, a developer wrote a test suite covering expected behavior, edge cases and a throughput target. After the first implementation, three tests fail. The developer investigates and finds that the failures are connected: order dates are parsed in the wrong timezone, the duplicate-detection key is built from that parsed date, and the daily totals are computed from the de-duplicated rows. A change to the date parsing will alter the keys, and a change to the keys will alter the totals.

How should the developer feed these failures back to Claude?

A. Share the first failure, wait for the fix, re-run the suite, and repeat for each of the remaining two failures.
B. Share all three failures in one detailed message that explains how the date, key and totals depend on each other.
C. Start a separate session for each failing test so that each of the three fixes is made with a clean context.
D. Ask Claude to rewrite the module from scratch without the failure output, to avoid anchoring on the first design.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: the three failures interact, since the duplicate key is built from the parsed date and the totals from the de-duplicated rows, so a fix to one changes the others. When fixes interact, the exam guide calls for addressing the issues in a single detailed message, here the three test failures together with their dependencies, so that Claude can design one coherent change. Option A treats connected failures as independent; each isolated fix is made without sight of the downstream effects and may be undone by the next. Option C goes further and hides the related failures from each fix altogether. Option D discards the test failures, which are the signal that test-driven iteration relies on to guide improvement. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.5 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Give Claude a way to verify its work • Common workflows — Work with tests

fields.Front:
Before asking Claude Code to build a CSV order-import module, a developer wrote a test suite covering expected behavior, edge cases and a throughput target. After the first implementation, three tests fail. The developer investigates and finds that the failures have nothing in common: a misspelled column name in the header validator, an off-by-one error in the pagination helper behind the progress report, and a missing null check in the export routine. The three functions sit in different files and share no data or code, and the whole suite runs in a few seconds.

How should the developer feed these failures back to Claude?

A. Share one failure at a time, re-running the suite after each fix before moving on to the next failure.
B. Write one message that describes all three failures and asks for one combined change, tested once at the end.
C. Ask Claude to re-read the whole module and correct anything that looks wrong, without the test output.
D. Relax the three failing assertions so that the suite passes, then revisit them after the module ships.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: the three failures are independent, in different files with no shared data or code, so no fix can affect another. For independent problems the exam guide calls for fixing them sequentially: share a failure, let Claude fix it, re-run the suite, which takes only seconds here, and move on, so that every change is confirmed on its own. Option B borrows the approach the guide reserves for interacting problems; with unrelated defects it bundles three changes into one tested only at the end, and if that run still fails it is harder to tell which change is at fault. Option C withholds the test failures, the precise signal that test-driven iteration depends on. Option D hides real defects by weakening the suite that defines correct behavior. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.5 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Give Claude a way to verify its work • Common workflows — Work with tests

fields.Front: Every push to a pull request triggers a team's CI pipeline, which runs claude -p to review the changes and posts the findings as inline comments. Each run is a separate invocation on a fresh runner. On a long-lived pull request, each run re-posts comments that an earlier run already made; most of the duplicates concern files that later commits keep touching, and some of the underlying issues have been fixed while others have not. Authors have started ignoring the review because they cannot tell new feedback from repeats. The team wants every push reviewed and unresolved findings kept visible. Which TWO changes to the re-run address this? (Select TWO.) A. Include the findings from earlier review runs in the context given to Claude for each re-run. B. Run the review only once, when the pull request is first opened, and skip all of the later pushes. C. Instruct Claude to report only issues that are new or that remain unaddressed since earlier runs. D. Limit each re-run to the files changed by the latest push, leaving other files out of the review.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and C. Options A and C are correct together: each run starts on a fresh runner with no knowledge of what was posted before, so it reports everything it finds again. Supplying the earlier findings as context (A) lets Claude see what has been raised, and the instruction to report only new or still-unaddressed issues (C) tells it what to do with that knowledge; either one alone leaves duplicates, since the instruction has nothing to compare against without the findings, and the findings change nothing without the instruction. Option B ends the duplicates by abandoning the requirement to review every push. Option D still re-reviews the files that later commits keep touching, where most duplicates arise, and drops unresolved findings in untouched files from view. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Code Review — What you can tune • Run Claude Code programmatically — Basic usage

fields.Front: A team's CI job runs claude -p on each pull request to propose unit tests for the changed code and posts them as a review comment. The job's prompt contains only the diff and the changed source files, and the run is configured without file-reading tools, so Claude sees nothing else in the repository. The repository's CLAUDE.md already documents the team's testing standards and shared fixtures, and reviewers find the proposed tests well written. Their complaint is different: about half of them repeat scenarios that the module's existing test file already covers, so reviewers cross-check every suggestion by hand. What change best addresses the complaint? A. Add a rule to CLAUDE.md stating that proposed tests must never duplicate scenarios the suite already covers. B. Include the existing test files for the changed modules in the context given to Claude for each run. C. Lower the number of proposed tests per pull request to five so that fewer duplicates reach reviewers. D. Add a second claude -p pass that rates each proposed test for quality and drops the low scorers.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct: the proposals are well written but duplicate existing coverage, and the run sees only the diff and the changed source files, so Claude has no way to know which scenarios the suite already tests. Putting the existing test files for the changed modules in context lets test generation skip what is covered and propose what is missing. Option A states the goal without supplying the information needed to meet it; a rule against duplication cannot be followed blind. Option C trims volume without regard to which suggestions are repeats, so duplicates still arrive and useful tests may be cut. Option D filters on quality, which reviewers already find acceptable, and the rating pass would be just as unaware of the existing tests. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Common workflows — Work with tests • Run Claude Code programmatically — Basic usage • CLI reference — CLI flags

fields.Front: A team's CI job runs claude -p on each pull request to propose unit tests for the changed code and posts them as a review comment. The job runs from a checkout of the repository and already includes the existing test files for the changed modules, so duplicates are rare. The reviewers' complaint is about value: many proposed tests assert trivial things such as a getter returning what was just set, build database records by hand instead of using the shared factories in tests/fixtures/, and ignore the team's expectation that each test cover a business behavior. None of these expectations is written down anywhere in the repository. What change best addresses the complaint? A. Add more of the repository's existing test files to the context so that Claude has a larger sample to imitate. B. Pass --output-format json with --json-schema so that each proposed test arrives in a fixed structure. C. Cap the number of proposed tests per pull request so that reviewers have fewer weak suggestions to reject. D. Document the testing standards, valuable-test criteria and fixtures in CLAUDE.md so that each run has them.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct: the weak proposals trace to expectations that are written down nowhere, namely which tests the team considers valuable, that each should cover a business behavior and that shared factories exist in tests/fixtures/. CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for giving CI-invoked Claude Code that project context, so documenting the standards, the criteria and the fixtures there improves what every run proposes. Option A leaves Claude to infer the standards from samples, when duplicates, the problem that existing tests in context solve, are already rare. Option B fixes the shape of the output, not its substance. Option C reduces the count without making any remaining test more valuable. Currency note (Oct 2026): claude -p loads CLAUDE.md unless it runs with --bare, which current docs recommend for scripted calls and say will become the default for -p. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Claude Code GitHub Actions — Define project standards in CLAUDE.md • Run Claude Code programmatically — Start faster with bare mode • Claude Code GitLab CI/CD — CLAUDE.md configuration

fields.Front:
An automated reviewer built on Claude Code runs on every pull request in a repository. Developers were dismissing many of its comments, mostly style preferences and objections to patterns the codebase uses deliberately. To fix this, an engineer appended one line to the review prompt: "Be conservative. Only report findings you are highly confident in." Two weeks later the share of dismissed comments is almost unchanged, and the dismissed ones are still style preferences and local patterns. Pull requests in this repository are small, usually one or two files.

What is the most likely reason the added line did not help?

A. It sets a general bar without saying which kinds of issue to report or skip, so the model still decides what a finding is.
B. It was appended at the end of the prompt, and review instructions are only followed when they come in the first paragraph.
C. The diffs are too large for a single pass, so the model has lost track of the line by the time it reaches the later files.
D. The model is well calibrated, so the dismissed comments must be valid problems that the developers are misjudging.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A identifies the gap. The dismissed comments are a kind of finding, style preferences and deliberate local patterns, and the added line says nothing about kinds. It asks for confidence, and the model can be entirely confident that a name departs from a style convention. What changes the outcome is categorical criteria that state which issues to report (bugs, security) and which to skip. Option B describes a placement rule that does not exist. Option C does not fit the facts, since the pull requests are one or two files. Option D treats self-reported confidence as proof of validity, although the dismissed comments are exactly the categories developers do not want. Currency note (Oct 2026): current model prompting pages add that newer models may follow such a line literally and leave real findings unreported, and they too recommend stating a concrete bar. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Prompting Claude Opus 4.8 — Code review harnesses • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct

fields.Front:
A nightly Claude Code job in a CI pipeline reviews changed files with the instruction "check that comments and docstrings are accurate." A typical run produces about 50 findings. Maintainers act on the three or four in which a docstring promises behavior the function no longer has, such as "returns an empty list on failure" above code that raises an exception. They close the rest without action: requests for more detail, rewording suggestions, and remarks that a comment is vague.

Which revised instruction best matches what the maintainers act on?

A. Check that comments and docstrings are accurate, and be conservative: report only what you are highly confident about.
B. Check that comments and docstrings are accurate, complete and clearly worded, and list the most serious ones first.
C. Flag a comment or docstring only when the behavior it claims contradicts what the code below it actually does.
D. Check that comments and docstrings are accurate, and report no more than five findings in any one nightly run.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Maintainers act only on findings in which the documented behavior and the real behavior disagree. Option C turns that into an explicit criterion, so wording, completeness and vagueness stop being reportable at all. "Accurate" on its own is open to interpretation, which is why terse or vague comments are being flagged. Option A keeps the vague criterion and adds a general confidence bar; the model can be entirely confident that a comment is vague. Option B widens the scope to completeness and wording, the very findings maintainers close, and ordering them does not remove them. Option D caps the volume arbitrarily: the five that survive may be rewording suggestions, while a real contradiction may be among those dropped. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct • Code Review — What you can tune

fields.Front:
A CI job runs Claude Code on every pull request and posts findings in four categories: security, null handling, resource leaks and naming. The prompt gives explicit criteria for the first three; for naming it says only "follow team conventions," because those conventions were never written down. Last month developers dismissed 6% of security findings, 8% of null-handling findings, 9% of resource-leak findings and 71% of naming findings. Dismissal notes increasingly read "bot noise," and two confirmed injection findings were closed unread. Writing the naming conventions down will take several weeks.

What should the team do first?

A. Add "be conservative and report high-confidence findings" to the prompt, so that the four categories become more selective.
B. Switch off the naming category for now, keep the other three running, and restore it once its criteria are written.
C. Leave the four categories posting while the conventions are written, since a naming finding takes one click to dismiss.
D. Suspend the review job until each category has been re-measured against a labeled sample of past pull requests.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. The false positives sit in one category: 71% of naming findings are dismissed against 6% to 9% elsewhere, and that noise is already leading developers to close accurate security findings unread. Option B removes the source of distrust at once, keeps the three precise categories working, and gives the team the weeks it needs to write real naming criteria before the category returns. Option A is a general instruction that supplies no criteria; the naming prompt would still say only "follow team conventions," and the accurate categories might report less. Option C leaves the noisy category undermining confidence in the accurate ones for several more weeks. Option D discards three categories that are working, security among them, to fix a problem confined to the fourth. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Code Review — What you can tune • Prompting Claude Opus 4.8 — Code review harnesses

fields.Front:
Every pull request in a repository is reviewed by a CI job that runs Claude Code and posts findings under four categories: security, null handling, resource leaks and naming. Over the last month developers dismissed between 38% and 44% of the findings in each of the four. The dismissed comments include unused-variable remarks filed under security, formatting preferences filed as bugs, and objections to a helper pattern that the repository uses on purpose. The entire review prompt is one sentence: "Review this diff and report anything a senior engineer might question."

What should the team change first?

A. Switch off whichever category has the highest dismissal rate for now, and restore it once its prompt has been improved.
B. Add an instruction to be conservative and to report only what a senior engineer would be highly confident about.
C. Have the model attach a confidence score to each finding, and post only the findings that score above a set threshold.
D. Rewrite the prompt to say which issues to report, such as bugs and security flaws, and which to skip, such as style.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Dismissals run at 38% to 44% in every category, and the one-sentence prompt never says what counts as a finding, so the model reports formatting preferences and intentional local patterns alongside real defects. Option D supplies the missing definition: specific kinds of issue to report (bugs, security flaws) and to skip (minor style, patterns the repository uses deliberately). Option A fits noise that is confined to one category; here none stands out, so disabling the worst one leaves the other three almost as noisy. Option B adds a general bar without saying which kinds of issue clear it. Option C filters on self-reported confidence, which does not separate a confidently stated style preference from a confidently stated bug, so the same mix of comments survives the threshold. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Prompting Claude Opus 4.8 — Code review harnesses • Code Review — What you can tune • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct

fields.Front: A pull-request review step run with Claude Code in CI labels each finding critical, major or minor, and a merge gate blocks on critical. Developers agree that the findings themselves are accurate, but the labels are not consistent. A SQL string built from request parameters in a public handler was rated major; the same construction in a one-off internal migration script was rated critical. The team's own reviewers would rate the first critical and the second minor, because only the first can be reached by untrusted input. The prompt's only guidance is "rate each finding by how serious it is." Which change is most likely to make the labels consistent? A. Define each level in the prompt with explicit criteria and a short code example of a finding that belongs at that level. B. Assign severity in post-processing from a fixed table that maps each finding category to exactly one of the levels. C. Have a second Claude instance rate every finding independently, and keep whichever of the two labels is higher. D. Tell the model to be conservative and to reserve the critical label for findings it is highly confident about.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. The findings are right, but nothing tells the model what separates the levels: the prompt says only to rate "how serious" each one is, so the same construction receives different labels. Option A writes down the rule the team actually applies, for example that reachability by untrusted input is what makes a finding critical, and anchors every level with a concrete code example, which is what yields consistent classification. Option B cannot express that rule, because both findings belong to one category yet deserve different levels. Option C doubles the cost while giving neither instance a definition, and keeping the higher label would block more merges. Option D confuses confidence with severity and adds one more undefined term. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.1 References: • Code Review — What you can tune • Prompting best practices — Use examples effectively

fields.Front:
A Claude Code review step in CI keeps flagging intentional idioms in a repository as defects: a retry wrapper that deliberately swallows one specific timeout exception, a module-level cache guarded by a lock, and test fixtures that open real sockets. Each time developers complained, an engineer added the exact file and function to a "do not flag" list in the prompt. The list has grown to 40 entries. Every newly written module that uses one of the same idioms is flagged until someone adds it to the list by name.

Which change best addresses the recurring problem?

A. Keep extending the list, and add a nightly job that appends a new entry for every finding that developers dismissed.
B. Replace the list with a few contrasting examples that pair an acceptable idiom with a real defect and explain why.
C. Tell the model to be conservative and to skip anything that could plausibly be an intentional design decision.
D. Remove error-handling and concurrency checks from the review altogether, so that these idioms can no longer be flagged.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. A list of named files and functions can only match what has already been listed, which is why each new module that uses the same idiom is flagged all over again. Option B teaches the distinction itself: a few examples that set an acceptable idiom beside a genuine defect, with the reason for each verdict, let the model generalize that judgment to code it has not seen. Option A automates the same matching and always lags one complaint behind. Option C swaps the list for a vague bar that gives no way to tell a deliberate swallow from a careless one, so real defects would be skipped as well. Option D ends the false positives by ending detection of genuine error-handling and concurrency bugs. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.2 References: • Prompting best practices — Use examples effectively • Prompting best practices — Add context to improve performance

fields.Front: In a multi-agent research system, a document-analysis subagent extracts sample_size, study_design and funding_source from each paper into a structured record. Its prompt describes the three fields in detail. For papers with a labeled Methods section the records are correct. For roughly a third of papers, which report these details in the abstract, in running prose or in a footnote, the fields come back null. A manual check of 40 such papers finds the values stated in the text of 37. What is the most effective change? A. Mark all three fields as required and non-nullable in the schema, so that the subagent must return a value for each. B. Send every record that contains a null back to the subagent with an error message until all three fields are filled. C. Cut each paper into fixed-size chunks, run the extraction on each chunk separately, and merge the partial records. D. Add a few examples of papers with different layouts, each showing where the values appeared and the correct record.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. The values are present in 37 of the 40 checked papers; the subagent misses them because they are not where a Methods heading would put them. Detailed field descriptions have not fixed that, so the stronger tool is a small set of examples that demonstrate extraction from varied structures: details embedded in an abstract, in prose, in a footnote. Option D does this. Option A forces a value for every field, which invites fabrication for the papers that really do omit one and still does not show where to look. Option B repeats the request with no new guidance and pushes the model to fill fields that may be absent. Option C treats a layout problem as a length problem and creates partial records that then have to be reconciled. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.2 References: • Prompting best practices — Use examples effectively • Get structured output from agents — Error handling

fields.Front: A support resolution agent built with the Claude Agent SDK chooses among lookup_order, process_refund and escalate_to_human. Each tool description already states its inputs, typical requests and boundaries, and the agent chooses correctly on clear requests. Its errors cluster on one kind of message: a customer wants money back for an item that stopped working some weeks after purchase. Policy treats these as refunds within 30 days of purchase and as warranty cases for the human team after that, and the system prompt already explains this in a paragraph. On these messages the agent still refunds some and escalates others without checking the order date. Which addition to the system prompt is most likely to fix this? A. Twenty examples of routine requests, such as tracking questions and simple returns, each paired with the right tool call. B. The existing policy paragraph repeated at the top and at the bottom of the prompt in capital letters, marked critical. C. Three examples of these messages, each showing the tool that was called and why the two alternatives were not used. D. A longer description for each of the three tools that restates the inputs and typical requests it already lists.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Selection is already right on clear requests and the descriptions already draw the boundaries, so the remaining errors come from one ambiguous kind of message on which a written policy is applied inconsistently. Option C targets exactly that: a few examples of the ambiguous case, each showing the action taken and why the plausible alternatives were rejected (look up the order first, because its date decides between a refund and a warranty escalation), give the agent a worked decision to generalize from. Option A adds tokens for cases the agent already handles. Option B repeats an instruction that is already present; emphasis does not show how to apply it. Option D would help if the descriptions were thin, but they are not. Currency note (Oct 2026): the guide speaks of 2 to 4 targeted examples; the current prompting page suggests 3 to 5. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.2 References: • Prompting best practices — Use examples effectively • Define tools — Best practices for tool definitions

fields.Front: An extraction pipeline classifies scanned legal documents through a tool whose schema has a contract_type enum with the values lease, employment, nda, services and other, plus a contract_type_detail string that is filled in when the type is other. A weekly job reads the other records to propose new enum values. About 5% of scans are fragments, such as a lone signature page, from which the type cannot be determined. The model gives some fragments whichever named type looks closest and files the remainder under other with a guessed detail, so the weekly job is proposing categories that do not exist. Which schema change addresses the fragments? A. Add an unclear value to the enum, so that the model can state that a scan does not show what type it is. B. Remove other and its detail field, so that every scan has to be assigned one of the four named contract types. C. Change contract_type to a free-text string, so that the model can describe each scan in its own words. D. Mark contract_type_detail as required, so that the model has to justify whichever type it has chosen.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. A fragment is not a new kind of contract; it is a document whose type cannot be told from what was scanned. The schema gives the model no way to say so, so it either forces a named type or misuses other, which exists for real types outside the list. Option A adds the missing value: unclear for ambiguous cases, leaving other with its detail string to do its own job of extending the categories. Option B removes the only unforced choice, so every fragment receives a wrong named type. Option C gives up the fixed values that routing and the weekly job depend on. Option D demands a justification while still making the model pick a type, so it would return a plausible detail for a guess. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3 References: • Structured outputs — JSON Schema limitations • Tool use with Claude — When Claude uses tools • Get structured output from agents — Error handling

fields.Front: A pipeline extracts invoice_date, due_date and amount from supplier invoices through a tool with a strict JSON schema, in which the dates are typed as strings and the amount as a number. Every response conforms to the schema. The accounts-payable import nevertheless rejects 9% of the records because it cannot parse their dates, which arrive as "03/04/2026", "4 March 2026" or "2026-03-04" depending on how the supplier printed them. An audit also finds amounts printed as "1.250,00" by European suppliers returned as 1.25. What is the most effective change? A. Mark all three fields as required in the schema, so that the model can no longer leave out a date or an amount. B. Raise max_tokens, so that the model has room to write each date and amount in more than one format. C. Send each rejected record back with the import error, and repeat until the accounts-payable import accepts it. D. Keep the schema, and add rules to the prompt for the output date format and for reading decimal commas.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. The schema is doing its job: every response has the right fields and types. What varies is how the source writes its values, and a schema cannot decide whether "03/04/2026" means March or April or how a decimal comma should be read. Option D keeps the schema and puts the missing rules in the prompt, for example ISO 8601 output and how to interpret European number formats, so values are normalized at extraction. Option A targets missing fields, and nothing is missing. Option B addresses truncation, which is not happening, and each field holds a single value in any case. Option C spends a second request on every rejected record and never sees the misread amounts, because 1.25 is a valid number that the import accepts. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.3 References: • Strict tool use • Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct • Structured outputs — Why use structured outputs

fields.Front: An invoice-extraction service returns each invoice through a tool with a strict JSON schema, so every response parses and validates. An audit nevertheless finds that for 3% of invoices the extracted line_items amounts do not add up to the extracted total. In some of these cases the model misread a line item; in others the supplier's printed total is itself wrong. Nothing in the pipeline identifies the affected invoices until someone reconciles the accounts weeks later. Which design lets the pipeline catch these invoices at extraction time? A. Add a prompt instruction that tells the model to adjust the line-item amounts until they add up to the invoice total. B. Extract the printed figure as stated_total and the line-item sum as calculated_total, and flag any difference. C. Tighten the schema so that total and every line-item amount are required fields with the type number. D. Run every extraction three times, and accept the total that is returned by at least two of the three runs.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. These records are well formed and wrong: a strict schema removes syntax and type errors, but it cannot tell whether the numbers agree with one another. Option B makes the disagreement visible by capturing both the total as printed and the total implied by the line items, so a simple comparison flags every invoice where they differ, whichever side is at fault. Option A hides the discrepancy by altering extracted data, and it would "correct" line items even when the printed total is the wrong figure. Option C restates constraints that are already met, since every response validates today. Option D triples the cost and checks only whether runs agree with each other on one number, not whether the line items support it. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.4 References: • Strict tool use • Structured outputs — Why use structured outputs

fields.Front: A finance team extracts payment_terms from supplier contracts into a structured record. In about 4% of contracts the document contradicts itself: the summary page says "Net 30" while clause 7.2 says "Net 45." The extraction returns one of the two values with nothing to mark the disagreement, and later checks find that the value returned was the wrong one in roughly half of these contracts. Nobody can say in advance which part of such a contract is authoritative; the legal group decides that case by case. How should the extraction handle these contracts? A. Instruct the model to take whichever value appears first in the document, so that its choice is at least predictable. B. Make payment_terms nullable, and have the model return null whenever it finds more than one candidate value. C. Add a conflict_detected boolean and record both values, so that these contracts are routed for a decision. D. Send the record back with a validation error, and repeat until the model returns the value that finance expects.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. The source itself is inconsistent, and which statement governs is a legal judgment the pipeline cannot make. Option C keeps the extraction honest: a conflict_detected flag with both values recorded shows that the document disagrees with itself and gives the legal group what it needs to decide. Option A makes the choice predictable but no more correct, and it still hides the conflict from everyone downstream. Option B does signal a problem, but it throws away both values and makes a conflicting contract indistinguishable from one that states no terms at all. Option D has nothing to correct: the output is not malformed, and no retry can settle a contradiction that lies in the document. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.4 References: • Structured outputs • Reduce hallucinations — Basic hallucination minimization strategies

fields.Front: A CI review step built on Claude Code posts structured findings on pull requests; each finding has file, line, category, severity and message. Developers dismiss about a third of the findings with one click and no comment. An engineer who wants to cut the false positives exports three months of dismissed findings but cannot see what they have in common: the messages are free text, and a category value such as error-handling covers dozens of different code constructs. Which change would make the dismissal data most useful for improving the prompt? A. Add a confidence field to every finding, and hide the findings that fall below a threshold that is retuned monthly. B. Require developers to type at least one sentence of justification before the dismiss button will close a finding. C. Post only the three highest-severity findings on each pull request, so that fewer findings are there to be dismissed. D. Add a detected_pattern field that names the code construct behind each finding, and group dismissals by it.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. The engineer's obstacle is that nothing in a finding records what triggered it, so dismissals cannot be grouped. Option D adds a detected_pattern field to the team's findings schema that names the construct, such as an empty catch block or a broad exception handler. Dismissal rates can then be computed per construct, and the prompt corrected for the specific ones developers reject. Option A hides findings without revealing which constructs are the false positives, so the prompt cannot be corrected and real issues under the threshold are lost. Option B adds friction to every dismissal and yields more free text of the kind that is already hard to analyze; developers may simply stop responding. Option C cuts volume blindly and leaves the cause of the false positives unknown. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.4 References: • Run Claude Code programmatically — Get structured output • Code Review — Rate and reply to findings

fields.Front: A procurement pipeline extracts purchase-order data from supplier emails through an extraction tool and validates each record with Pydantic before loading it into the ERP system. One record fails validation with two errors: delivery_date is "the 3rd of next month" where an ISO date is required, and line_items is a single comma-separated string where an array of objects is required. The email itself lists every line item with its quantity and price, says "delivery on the 3rd of next month," and carries its sent date in the header. What should the pipeline do with this record? A. Send the same request again unchanged, on the expectation that a second attempt will come back in the right shape. B. Route the record straight to a human reviewer, since a record that has failed validation once will fail again. C. Send a follow-up request that contains the source email, the failed extraction and the two specific validation errors. D. Loosen the Pydantic model to accept free-text dates and string line items, and let the ERP import sort them out.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Everything the validator asks for is in the email: the items, quantities and prices are listed, and the sent date fixes what "the 3rd of next month" means. The failures are a format mismatch and a structural error, the kind a retry can correct once the model is told exactly what was wrong. Option C supplies the original document, the failed extraction and the specific errors, so the model can repair those two fields instead of starting blind. Option A gives the model no new information, so the same output is likely to come back. Option B spends reviewer time on a record the model can fix itself. Option D lets malformed data into the ERP system, where it is harder to catch. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.4 References: • Handle tool calls — Handling errors with is_error • Get structured output from agents • Prompting best practices — Chain complex prompts

fields.Front: Supplier emails are turned into purchase-order records by a procurement pipeline: an extraction tool fills in the record, and Pydantic validation runs before anything is loaded into the ERP system. One record fails with a single error: po_number is null, and the loader needs a value. The email's only mention of the order reads "as per the purchase order attached to our message of last Tuesday." That earlier message and its attachment were never given to the pipeline, and no order number appears anywhere in the email. What should the pipeline do with this record? A. Skip the retry, record the number as missing, and route the record so that the referenced attachment is obtained. B. Send a follow-up request that contains the email, the failed extraction and the specific validation error. C.
