Make po_number a required, non-nullable string in the tool schema, so that the model has to return a value. D. Add few-shot examples of emails that state a purchase-order number, so that the model learns where to look for one.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. The number is not in the email; it exists only in an earlier attachment that the pipeline never received. A retry hands the model the same source, so no error message can make the value appear, and pressing for one invites an invented number. Option A accepts null as the honest result and sends the record to where the missing document can be fetched. Option B is the right response to a format or structural error, where the information is present but badly expressed; here it would only repeat the search. Option C takes away the model's way of saying "absent" and so produces a fabricated value that passes validation. Option D teaches the model where such numbers usually sit, which does not help when there is none to find. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.4 References: • Get structured output from agents — Error handling • Reduce hallucinations — Basic hallucination minimization strategies

fields.Front:
An insurer extracts structured data from uploaded claim documents with Claude. Each document's extraction must be available to adjusters within 36 hours of upload. To halve the model cost, the team moved the work to the Message Batches API and submits everything received that day in one batch at midnight. Some documents are missing the deadline. For planning purposes the team assumes that a batch may take the full 24-hour processing window to return its results.

Which submission schedule keeps the worst case inside the deadline at the lowest cost?

A. Keep the single midnight batch, and poll its status every five minutes so that the results are collected sooner.
B. Submit a batch every 16 hours, which cuts the longest wait before submission by a third compared with today.
C. Move these documents to the synchronous Messages API, so that each extraction comes back within seconds.
D. Submit a batch every 8 hours, so that the longest wait before submission plus 24 hours of processing is 32 hours.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. The worst case is a document that arrives just after a batch has gone: it waits one full submission interval and then up to 24 hours for results. With a single midnight batch that is 48 hours. Option D brings it to 8 + 24 = 32 hours, inside the 36-hour deadline with room to collect the results, and every request still gets the batch discount. Option A changes neither term of the sum; polling only tells you sooner that a batch has ended. Option B gives 16 + 24 = 40 hours, which is still late. Option C meets the deadline but gives up the 50% saving on a workload that can tolerate the wait. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs add that most batches finish within an hour, and that a request the batch has not reached by its 24-hour expiration comes back as expired, without a result. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.5 References: • Batch processing — Batch limitations • Batch processing — Pricing • Batch processing — Retrieving batch results

fields.Front:
Claim documents uploaded to an insurer are run through Claude to extract structured data. A new fraud-screening step needs each document's extraction within 4 hours of upload. The extraction currently goes through the Message Batches API at half the standard price, and the team's dashboard shows that most of its batches finish in under an hour. A teammate proposes keeping the batch discount for the fraud-screening documents by submitting a small batch every 30 minutes.

Which approach meets the four-hour requirement?

A. Submit a batch every 30 minutes as proposed, since nearly all of the team's batches finish in well under four hours.
B. Send these documents through the synchronous Messages API as they arrive, and pay the standard price for them.
C. Keep batching these documents, and send those that a keyword pre-check flags as suspicious through the synchronous API.
D. Keep the batch, and have each request call a tool that pushes its result to the fraud system when it is done.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Batch processing carries no latency guarantee: most batches finish within an hour, but any batch may take up to 24 hours, so no submission interval can promise four. A requirement that has to hold every time belongs on the synchronous API, which is what Option B chooses, at the standard price for this subset only. Option A relies on typical behavior to meet a hard deadline. Option C leaves the documents that the pre-check does not flag on the batch path, where any of them can take up to 24 hours, and the requirement covers each document's extraction, not just the ones a keyword check happens to flag. Option D cannot work, because a batched request cannot run your tool and carry on; the tool_use block just sits in the results until the batch ends. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs say Anthropic-run server tools such as web search do loop inside a batched request; tools that your own application executes still cannot return results mid-request. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.5 References: • Batch processing — Batch limitations • Batch processing — FAQ • Batch processing — Server tools and the agentic loop

fields.Front:
A platform team plans a one-time audit of 60,000 source files for unsafe deserialization, and it will use the Message Batches API to halve the cost. The audit prompt was drafted this morning and has been tried on four files, all of them from one Python service. The repository also holds Go, Java, TypeScript and Kotlin code, along with generated files and test fixtures. The audit has no deadline tighter than the end of the month. Results for a batch become available only when the whole batch has finished processing.

What should the team do before it submits the full set of files?

A. Run the prompt on a sample that spans the languages and file types, refine it, and then submit the full set.
B. Submit all 60,000 files now, and afterwards fix the prompt and resubmit the files whose results are unusable.
C. Divide the files into 600 batches of 100 and submit them together, so that the results come back in smaller files.
D. Send every file through the synchronous Messages API instead, so that each response can be read as it arrives.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. A prompt tried on four files from one service has not met most of what the full set contains, and a batch offers no chance to adjust midway, because results arrive only once the whole batch has ended. Option A spends a little on a sample that covers each language and the unusual file types, so the gaps in the prompt show up before the large run and the full submission is far more likely to succeed in one pass. Option B finds the same gaps only after paying for 60,000 requests, and then pays again for every file that has to be resubmitted. Option C changes how the results are packaged; every file is still processed with the untested prompt. Option D gives up the batch discount on work that has no deadline pressure, and reading responses as they arrive is not a test of the prompt. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.5 References: • Batch processing — Best practices for effective batching • Best practices for Claude Code — Fan out across files • Batch processing — Pricing

fields.Front: A legal-operations team sends 10,000 contracts through the Message Batches API each night to extract key terms, and the custom_id of each request is the contract's document ID. When this morning's batch ended, 9,640 results had the type succeeded and 360 had the type errored. Every errored result carries an invalid_request_error whose message says that the prompt is too long. The 360 contracts turn out to be master agreements with several hundred pages of annexes. Which two actions should the team take to finish the extraction? (Select TWO.) A. Collect the custom_id of every errored result, and build the next batch from those 360 contracts only. B. Split each of the 360 contracts into sections that fit the context window before the requests are resubmitted. C. Resubmit all 10,000 requests in one new batch, and keep the newest result recorded for each custom_id. D. Resubmit the 360 requests with a higher max_tokens value and leave the text of the contracts unchanged.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and B. The batch did its job for 9,640 contracts; only the 360 errored requests need work, and they failed for a reason that will recur unless the requests change. Option A uses the custom_id on each result to pick out exactly those contracts, which is what the field is for, since results are not returned in the order of the requests. Option B removes the cause: an input larger than the context window is rejected however often it is sent, so each long contract has to be divided into sections that fit, with the extracted pieces merged afterwards. Option C pays again for 9,640 extractions that already succeeded and fails again on the same 360. Option D raises the wrong limit, because max_tokens caps the length of the response and does nothing for an oversized prompt. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.5 References: • Batch processing — Retrieving batch results • Context windows — Context window overflow behavior • Batches (API reference)

fields.Front:
A CI job reviews large pull requests with Claude in two kinds of pass. In the per-file pass, a separate instance examines each changed file on its own and reports local problems. In the integration pass, one instance receives only the changed function signatures, the places where those functions are called, and the shared data models, and it reports problems that span files. The team wants every review to confirm, from now on, that each function which parses a request body handles malformed input.

Where does the new check belong?

A. Add it to the integration pass, because that pass is the one that sees how the changed files fit together.
B. Add it to both passes, so that every function is checked twice and the two sets of findings can be compared.
C. Add it to the per-file pass, because whether a function handles bad input can be judged from its own file alone.
D. Merge the two passes into one request that reads every changed file in full, so that nothing is out of view.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. What decides the placement is the scope of the check: whether a parsing function copes with malformed input can be read from the function's own body, so it is a local issue. Option C puts it in the pass that reads each file closely and on its own. Option A gives it to an instance that sees signatures, call sites and data models but no function bodies, so it could not tell whether the handling exists. Option B doubles the work, and two passes that look at different material would return duplicate and sometimes contradictory findings about the same function. Option D rebuilds the single large review that the split was designed to replace: one request holding every file spreads attention thin, and the per-file pass already has all the context this check needs. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.6 References: • Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows — Review every changed file and write one summary • Code Review — How reviews work

fields.Front:
Claude reviews large pull requests in a CI job that is split into two kinds of pass. The per-file pass runs one instance per changed file, and each instance sees that file alone and looks for local defects. The integration pass runs a single instance that is given just the changed function signatures, their call sites and the shared data models, and it looks for defects that cross file boundaries. After an incident in which a function began returning a list of records instead of a single record, the team wants every review to confirm that when a function's return type changes, each of its callers has been updated to match.

Where does the new check belong?

A. Add it to the per-file pass, because each instance there reads its file closely enough to notice a stale call.
B. Add it to the integration pass, because a function and the code that calls it usually sit in different files.
C. Add it to both passes, so that every call site is checked twice and the two sets of findings can be compared.
D. Merge the two passes into one request that reads every changed file in full, so that nothing is out of view.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. What decides the placement is the scope of the check: a function and its callers usually live in different files, so a stale caller is a cross-file issue. Option B puts it in the pass that is given the changed signatures together with their call sites, which is exactly the pairing needed to see that a caller still assumes the old return type. Option A asks an instance that sees one file to judge a call against a definition it has not been shown, so it can only guess. Option C keeps that guesswork and adds duplicate, possibly conflicting findings from two passes. Option D would have the material, but it rebuilds the single large review that the split was designed to replace, with attention spread thin across every file, when the integration pass already receives what the check requires. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.6 References: • Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows — Review every changed file and write one summary • Code Review — How reviews work

fields.Front: A developer has Claude Code implement a caching layer for a multi-tenant API over a long session. Early in the session Claude reasoned that the cache key did not need to include the tenant ID, and it wrote the code that way. When the implementation is finished, the developer asks in that same session for a careful review of the changes, and the review reports no problems. A colleague later finds that one tenant can be served another tenant's cached response. Other subtle defects have slipped through the same review step. Which change to the review step is most likely to catch defects of this kind? A. Give the same session a detailed self-review checklist that tells Claude to re-examine every decision it made. B. Enable extended thinking for the review request, so that Claude reasons at greater length before it answers. C. Resume the session with --fork-session, and run the review in the fork so that it has a new session ID. D. Run the review in a second Claude instance that receives the diff and the requirements but not the session.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. The reviewer here is the author: the session still holds the reasoning that produced the cache key, so a review inside it tends to accept that reasoning again instead of questioning it. Option D removes that context, because a second instance that sees only the diff and the requirements must judge the code on its own terms and has no conclusion of its own to defend. Option A adds instructions but leaves the same context in place, where the justification for the key is still there to be agreed with. Option B gives more reasoning to the same biased starting point. Option C changes the session ID only: a fork starts with a copy of the conversation's history, including the decision about the tenant ID. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs deprecate extended thinking with a fixed token budget on Claude 4.6 models and reject it on later ones, which use adaptive thinking. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.6 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Add an adversarial review step • Best practices for Claude Code — Run multiple Claude sessions • Work with sessions — Fork to explore alternatives

fields.Front:
An overnight Claude Code job reviews a 90-file release branch and produces about 120 findings by morning. Two engineers have an hour each to go through them before the release meeting. The findings are listed in file order with a severity, but nothing separates the ones the review is sure of from the ones that are speculative, and in past releases about half of the findings turned out not to be real. The team is unwilling to discard any finding unseen, because a few of the doubtful ones have been genuine defects.

Which addition to the pipeline makes the best use of the engineers' two hours?

A. Add an instruction to the review prompt that tells Claude to be conservative and report only what it is sure of.
B. Have the engineers read the first 60 findings in file order, and hold the remainder over until the next release.
C. Add a verification pass that rechecks each finding against the code and reports a confidence level used for routing.
D. Run the whole review three times, and keep only the findings that are reported by all three of the runs.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. What is missing is any signal of which findings deserve the engineers' limited time, and the team wants every finding kept. Option C adds a second pass that goes back to the code for each finding and attaches a confidence level, so the findings can be routed: the well-supported ones to the two engineers before the meeting, and the doubtful ones to a later queue or to the owner of the file, with none thrown away. Option A moves the filtering into the pass that is looking for problems, where a vague instruction either changes little or suppresses real defects along with the noise, and what it suppresses reaches nobody. Option B spends the two hours on an arbitrary half, ordered by file name and not by merit. Option D discards whatever is not reported three times, which the team has ruled out, at three times the cost. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.6 References: • Prompting Claude Opus 4.8 — Code review harnesses • Code Review — How reviews work

fields.Front:
A support assistant built on the Claude API handles billing conversations whose turns and tool results often outgrow the model's context window. To keep them inside it, the backend replaces every turn older than the latest eight with a running summary written by the model, and sends that summary plus the latest eight turns on each request. In one session a customer disputes three orders. Early on, the assistant confirms a refund of $87.43 on the first order, due by 14 March, and the customer says they expect a call if it is late. Forty turns later the summary reads "customer is owed a refund on a recent order", and the assistant tells the customer that a refund of "around $90" is on its way.

Which change best prevents this loss?

A. Summarize more often, so that each summary pass covers fewer turns and has less material to compress.
B. Stop summarizing, and send the complete transcript of the session on every request however long it grows.
C. Extract amounts, dates and order numbers into a case-facts block sent with every request, outside the summarized history.
D. Lower the temperature of the summarization call, so that each summary is worded more consistently than the one before.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. The exact refund amount, the due date and the customer's stated expectation were lost when older turns passed through the running summary: progressive summarization tends to condense figures and dates into vague phrases. Option C keeps those transactional facts for each of the three orders in a persistent block that is sent with every request and never passes through the summarizer, so the summary can stay loose without costing precision. Option A adds summary passes, so each fact is rewritten more often and blurs sooner. Option B removes the mechanism that keeps long sessions inside the context window; a request that exceeds the window is rejected by the API, and recall degrades as context grows. Option D makes the summary's wording more repeatable, but it does not change what a summary leaves out. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.1 References: • Effective context engineering for AI agents — Context engineering for long-horizon tasks • Context editing — When to use compaction • Context windows — Context window overflow behavior

fields.Front:
A support assistant built on the Claude API handles billing conversations that rarely run past ten turns, and no summarization is used. For each customer turn, the backend sends a request containing the system prompt, the tool definitions and only the newest customer message. In one session a customer gives an order number and explains that a refund of $87.43 was promised by 14 March; the assistant looks the order up and confirms both details. Two turns later the customer asks "So when will I get it?", and the assistant replies by asking which order the customer means.

Which change best fixes this?

A. Extract amounts, dates and order numbers into a case-facts block, and send that block with each request in place of the earlier turns.
B. Send the conversation so far, including earlier assistant turns and tool results, in the messages of every request.
C. Move the assistant to a model with a larger context window, so that earlier turns are no longer pushed out of the request.
D. Add a system prompt instruction telling the assistant to remember any order number that a customer has already supplied.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. The backend sends only the newest customer message, and the Messages API is stateless: the model sees nothing from earlier turns unless the request contains them. Option B sends the conversation so far, which is what lets "it" resolve to the order and the refund already discussed; at about ten turns this fits easily. Option A would carry a few values forward but would go on withholding the dialogue, and it adds an extraction step that suits long sessions whose history has to be summarized, which is not the case here. Option C addresses a limit that is not being reached: the earlier turns are never sent, so no window size brings them back. Option D asks the model to remember text that it is never given. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.1 References: • Using the Messages API — Multiple conversational turns • Context windows — How the context window works

fields.Front:
In a multi-agent research system, a coordinator agent joins the findings of fourteen search and analysis subagents, in the order they finish, into one input for a synthesis subagent. The combined input is long, but it fits well within the synthesis subagent's context window. Reviewing a month of reports, you find that findings from the first two and the last two subagent outputs appear reliably, while findings from outputs that sit in the middle of the input are often missing, whichever subtopics happen to land there.

Which change to the combined input best addresses this?

A. Shorten each subagent's output to its opening paragraph, and join the shortened outputs in the order in which they are returned.
B. Move the synthesis subagent to a model with a larger context window, and pass it the combined input in its present form.
C. Join the subagent outputs in a different random order on each run, and leave the content of each output unchanged.
D. Open the input with a summary of each subagent's key findings, and put the detailed results under explicit section headers.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Findings are dropped according to where they sit, not what they cover, and the input fits the window, so capacity is not the constraint. The exam guide calls this the "lost in the middle" effect: material at the start and end of a long input is processed reliably, while the middle may be omitted. Option D places a summary of every subagent's key findings in the reliable opening position and gives the detail explicit section headers. Option A removes most of the detail in order to fix a problem of position. Option B adds room that is not short. Option C changes which findings are overlooked on each run without reducing how many. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs do not use the term "lost in the middle"; they advise placing long documents at the top of a prompt with the query at the end, and they describe recall degrading as context grows. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.1 References: • Prompting best practices — Long context prompting • Context windows — How the context window works

fields.Front:
In a multi-agent research system, a coordinator agent joins the output of fourteen search and analysis subagents into one input for a synthesis subagent, whose report must attribute every claim to a source. Each subagent returns the full text of the pages it read, together with its step-by-step reasoning. The synthesis subagent runs with a fixed context budget, most of which is reserved for drafting the report. The combined input is about three times the remaining budget, so the coordinator cuts it off at the limit, and the findings of the last nine subagents never reach synthesis.

Which change best addresses this?

A. Have the subagents return key facts with citations and relevance scores as structured data, without page text or reasoning.
B. Have the coordinator write a prose summary of each subagent's output, and pass the fourteen summaries on to the synthesis subagent.
C. Open the combined input with the highest-priority subagent's output, and place the other outputs under explicit section headers.
D. Split synthesis into three runs that each receive a third of the combined input, and join the three partial reports end to end.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. The combined input is about three times what the synthesis subagent can accept, and most of that volume is page text and reasoning that synthesis does not need. Option A fixes this at the source: the upstream subagents return key facts with citations and relevance scores as structured data, which is the approach the exam guide gives for downstream agents with limited context budgets, and it keeps each claim tied to its source. Option B leaves the coordinator absorbing all fourteen verbose outputs, and prose summaries tend to drop figures and the attribution that the report requires. Option C reorders the material without shrinking it, so the cut-off happens anyway. Option D fits each third within the budget, but no run compares findings across thirds, so the result is three partial reports and not a synthesis. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.1 References: • Effective context engineering for AI agents — Context engineering for long-horizon tasks • Create custom subagents — Run parallel research • How we built our multi-agent research system — Benefits of a multi-agent system

fields.Front: The lookup_order tool of a customer support resolution agent built with the Claude Agent SDK returns the complete order record: more than forty fields, including warehouse codes, tax breakdowns and marketing attribution. To decide whether an item can be returned, the agent uses five of them: order ID, item, delivery date, price paid and return status. In sessions where a customer asks about several orders, most of the tokens in the conversation are order records, and transcripts show the agent quoting the delivery date of one order while discussing another. What is the most effective first step? A. Move the agent to a model with a larger context window, and keep returning the complete record for each order. B. Reduce each order lookup result to the five return-related fields before the result is added to the conversation. C. Add a system prompt instruction that lists the five return-related fields the agent should read in each order record. D. Summarize the conversation after each second order lookup, and replace the older order records with that summary.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Most of the conversation's tokens are order records, yet the agent needs only five of more than forty fields from each: tool results are accumulating out of proportion to their relevance, and the surplus crowds the details that matter. Option B trims each result to the return-related fields before it enters the conversation, for example in the tool's handler or in a hook that replaces the tool's output before the model sees it, so the clutter never accumulates. Option A makes room for the clutter without removing it, and more context is not automatically better. Option C leaves every field in context and relies on the model to ignore most of what it is given. Option D lets the full records in first and then compresses them, and summarizing is where exact dates and amounts tend to blur. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.1 References: • Writing effective tools for agents — with agents • How the agent loop works — What consumes context • Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks — Outputs

fields.Front: A customer support resolution agent built with the Claude Agent SDK can look up orders, issue refunds within policy and hand a conversation to staff through an escalate_to_human tool. A customer opens a chat with this message: "I have been waiting nine days longer than you promised and nobody has told me anything. This is ridiculous. Sort it out." The order is easy to find, and policy lets the agent offer a full refund or a free replacement for any delivery more than seven days late. How should the agent respond? A. Acknowledge the frustration, and offer the customer a choice between the full refund and the free replacement. B. Call escalate_to_human at once, and tell the customer that a member of staff will take over the conversation. C. Apologize for the delay, and offer the full refund together with a goodwill credit on the customer's next order. D. Look up the order and gather the full delivery history, then call escalate_to_human with a summary for staff.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. The customer is angry but has not asked for a person, and the remedy is one the agent is allowed to give: the order is easy to find and policy covers any delivery more than seven days late. Option A acknowledges the frustration and offers what the policy provides; escalation remains available if the customer then asks for a human. Option B treats tone as the trigger; the exam guide treats sentiment as an unreliable proxy for case complexity, and this case is simple. Option C lets tone change the remedy: policy provides a refund or a replacement, so a goodwill credit is an exception that the agent would be granting on its own authority. Option D does the investigation and then hands off a case that needs no handoff, which adds a wait for the customer and work for staff without changing the outcome. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.2 References: • Customer support agent — Establish success criteria • Building effective agents — A. Customer support

fields.Front: A customer support resolution agent built with the Claude Agent SDK can look up orders, issue refunds within policy and hand a conversation to staff through an escalate_to_human tool. A customer opens a chat with this message: "My order is nine days late. I am not going through this with a bot. Put me through to a person." The agent has not looked anything up. Policy lets it offer a full refund or a free replacement for any delivery more than seven days late, so it could probably settle the matter itself within a turn or two. What should the agent do first? A. Acknowledge the frustration and offer the refund or replacement, escalating only if the customer asks for a person a second time. B. Explain that the agent can settle a late delivery faster than staff can, and continue with the refund unless the customer objects. C. Look up the order and work out the cause of the delay, then call escalate_to_human with a full analysis for staff. D. Call escalate_to_human right away, passing on what the customer has said, without first investigating the order.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. The customer has explicitly asked for a person, and the exam guide treats that as an escalation trigger to honor immediately, without first attempting investigation, even where the agent could resolve the issue itself. Option D hands the conversation over with what the customer has said. Option A is the right pattern for a customer who is only frustrated; applied here, it makes someone who has stated a preference state it twice. Option B argues with the request and proceeds on the customer's silence, which overrides a clearly stated choice. Option C delays the handoff for an investigation the customer did not ask for; passing on what is already known helps staff, but new analysis is not a condition of escalating. That the refund is within policy does not change the answer: the trigger is the request, not the difficulty of the case. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.2 References: • Customer support agent — Establish success criteria • Building effective agents — A. Customer support

fields.Front: Before it looks up orders or issues refunds, a customer support resolution agent built with the Claude Agent SDK verifies who it is talking to by calling a get_customer tool. A customer opens a chat giving only a full name and asking for a refund on a recent order. The tool returns three accounts under that name, each with a different email address and city. In test runs the agent continues with whichever account has the most recent order, and in several runs it has described another person's order to the customer. Which change best addresses this? A. Add a hook that reduces each get_customer result to its first match, so that later tools always receive a single customer ID. B. Instruct the agent to ask the customer for a further identifier, such as an email address, whenever a lookup returns several matches. C. Instruct the agent to show the customer the email address and city of each match, and to proceed with the one the customer picks. D. Instruct the agent to call escalate_to_human whenever a lookup returns several matches, so that staff confirm the identity.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Three accounts share the name, and the agent picks one by a heuristic, the most recent order, which is how another person's order came to be described. A name alone cannot settle which account is the customer's, so the agent should ask for a further identifier and continue only when exactly one account matches: Option B. Option A makes the guess deterministic without making it correct, since the first match is as arbitrary as the most recent one. Option C does ask the customer, but by disclosing other customers' email addresses and cities to someone whose identity is unverified. Option D sends staff a problem that one clarifying question would settle, which adds a wait and uses staff time on a case with no policy gap and no request for a person. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.2 References: • Handle approvals and user input — Handle clarifying questions • Customer support agent — Establish success criteria

fields.Front: The system prompt of a customer support resolution agent for an electronics retailer contains the full returns policy. The policy says an item bought on its own can be returned within 30 days for a refund of the price paid, and it says nothing about items bought as part of a discounted bundle. A customer writes politely to return only the headphones from a laptop-and-headphones bundle bought twelve days ago at a bundle discount. The order is easy to find, the agent can hand a conversation to staff, and its process_refund tool would accept any amount up to the order total. What should the agent do? A. Refund the headphones at the price they carry when sold separately, and confirm the return to the customer. B. Refund a proportional share of the bundle price, and flag the case for staff to review once the refund is issued. C. Escalate the request to a human agent, with a summary of the order and of what the customer is asking for. D. Decline the partial return, and tell the customer that the bundle is returnable as a whole within 30 days.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. The request is simple and the customer is calm, but the policy is silent on it: the 30-day rule covers items bought on their own and says nothing about part of a discounted bundle. The exam guide treats a policy gap as an escalation trigger in its own right, not only complex cases, so Option C is correct: staff decide, with the order and the request in front of them. Options A and B each apply a refund formula that the policy does not contain, and the two give different amounts, which shows that the policy does not settle the question; asking staff to review after the refund, as Option B does, leaves the agent's decision already made. Option D invents two rules from the same silence, a ban on partial returns and a right to return the whole bundle. That the process_refund tool would accept either amount shows only what the agent is able to do, not what the policy permits. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.2 References: • Customer support agent — Establish success criteria • Building effective agents — Agents

fields.Front: A team reviews conversations handled by a customer support resolution agent, which resolves most returns and billing questions itself and can hand off through an escalate_to_human tool. The review finds 300 conversations that should have reached a person but did not: in 190 the request was one the written policy does not cover, and in 110 the agent went back and forth for ten or more turns without getting closer to a resolution. In both groups the customers' messages were mostly neutral in tone, and the agent, when asked to rate its confidence, averaged 8.6 out of 10. The review also finds that the most negative messages come mainly from late-delivery complaints, which the agent resolves within policy. A colleague proposes escalating automatically whenever sentiment turns strongly negative or the agent's self-rated confidence falls below 5. What would this proposal most likely do? A. Escalate most of the 300, since conversations that go unresolved end up producing strongly negative customer sentiment. B. Escalate the 190 policy cases, since the agent rates its confidence lower when the written policy is silent. C. Escalate the 110 stalled cases, since ten turns without progress show up as a clear drop in sentiment. D. Escalate few of the 300, since neither signal fires on them, and hand off complaints the agent already resolves.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Both proposed signals are proxies, and the review's own numbers show that neither fires where it is needed: the 300 missed conversations were mostly neutral in tone, and the agent rated itself at 8.6 out of 10 on them. Option D follows: few of the 300 would be escalated, while the angriest messages, which come from late-delivery complaints the agent already resolves within policy, would be handed off. Option A assumes that unresolved cases turn negative, which the review contradicts. Option B assumes that the agent's confidence drops when policy is silent, but it was high in exactly those cases. Option C assumes that stalling shows up in sentiment, which it did not. The exam guide treats sentiment and self-reported confidence as unreliable proxies for case complexity; the triggers that fit this data are explicit ones, a request the policy does not cover or no meaningful progress. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.2 References: • Customer support agent — Establish success criteria • Building effective agents — Agents

fields.Front:
A multi-agent research system is producing a report on grid-scale battery storage with three sections: cost trends, safety incidents and recycling. Its search and analysis subagents returned well-sourced findings for cost trends and safety incidents. For recycling, the system's coordinator agent received structured error context: the two industry databases that hold the relevant data could not be reached after repeated attempts, and a single trade-press article was retrieved. The coordinator has decided to proceed with what it has.

How should the system's synthesis subagent structure its output?

A. Write the three sections in the same style, and close with a general sentence saying that some of the sources were unavailable.
B. Leave the recycling section out, and present cost trends and safety incidents as the report's complete findings.
C. Write the recycling section from the model's background knowledge, and bring it to the same depth as the other two.
D. Mark cost trends and safety incidents as well supported, and annotate recycling as a gap left by two unreachable databases.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Two sections rest on well-sourced findings; the third rests on one article because two databases could not be reached. A reader can act on the report only if it shows which is which. Option D annotates coverage section by section: what is well supported, and where there is a gap and why. Option A mentions a limitation without saying which section it affects, so the thin recycling section reads with the same authority as the others. Option B removes the thin section instead of marking it, so readers take a two-section report as the complete findings and lose both the one article that was retrieved and any sign that recycling data could not be reached. Option C fills the gap with unsourced material presented alongside sourced findings, which conceals the access failure and invites fabricated detail. Proceeding with partial results is reasonable here, provided that the output says where they are partial. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.3 References: • How we built our multi-agent research system — Production reliability and engineering challenges • Reduce hallucinations — Basic hallucination minimization strategies

fields.Front:
A web search subagent in a multi-agent research system is fetching five sources for the subtopic that a coordinator agent assigned to it. Four fetches succeed and yield usable findings. The fifth returns an HTTP 503 response with a header asking the client to retry after two seconds; the same site answered normally a minute earlier. The subagent can repeat a fetch with the tool it already has, and the coordinator, whose own tools do not include fetching pages, is waiting on this subagent and on three others that are running in parallel.

How should the subagent handle the failed fetch?

A. Return at once with structured error context for the fifth source, so that the coordinator can decide how to recover.
B. Return the four sources' findings as a completed task, and leave the fifth source out of the report to the coordinator.
C. Retry after the delay, and if the fetch keeps failing, return the four sources' findings with a note on what was attempted.
D. Retry after the delay, and if the fetch keeps failing, return a "search unavailable" status in place of any findings.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. A 503 with a two-second retry-after delay, from a site that answered a minute earlier, is a transient failure, and the subagent holds the tool that can repeat the fetch. The exam guide's pattern is local recovery first: retry where the failure happened, and propagate only what cannot be resolved, together with what was attempted and the partial results. That is Option C. Option A is accurate reporting sent too early; it pushes a two-second retry up to a coordinator that cannot fetch pages and would have to delegate the fetch to a fresh subagent. Option B hides the failure, so the coordinator would take four sources for full coverage. Option D retries, but then discards four good results behind a generic status that tells the coordinator nothing about what failed or what was tried. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.3 References: • How we built our multi-agent research system — Production reliability and engineering challenges • Handle tool calls — Handling errors with is_error • Give Claude custom tools — Handle errors

fields.Front: In a multi-agent research system, a coordinator agent asks a literature search subagent to find peer-reviewed studies published since 2024 on four-day school weeks and teacher retention. The subagent's query to an academic index times out after 30 seconds. The subagent returns structured error context to the coordinator: failure type timeout, the query it attempted, no partial results, and a note that a second index covering the same journals is available. Findings on the other subtopics have arrived from other subagents without problems, and a synthesis subagent will write the report from what the coordinator passes on. How should the coordinator respond? A. Record the subtopic as having zero published studies in the period, and pass that finding to the synthesis subagent. B. Choose a recovery route from the error context, and retry the query or search the second index accordingly. C. Stop the research run, and report the timeout to the user together with the findings gathered up to that point. D. Pass the error context to the synthesis subagent, and have it report the subtopic as one that was not searched.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. The subagent reports that the query timed out: the index was never searched, so nothing is known about what it holds. A timeout is an access failure, and it calls for a retry decision. The structured context gives the coordinator what it needs to make one: the failure type, the attempted query and an alternative index. Option B uses that context to attempt recovery; a coverage gap is reported only if both routes fail. Option A turns "could not search" into "nothing exists", which is the conclusion a valid empty result would support and a timeout does not. Option C ends the whole run over one failure although the other subtopics succeeded and a second index is available. Option D is honest about the gap but declares it too early: the synthesis subagent can only write up what it is given, so the recovery that the error context makes possible is never attempted. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.3 References: • How we built our multi-agent research system — Production reliability and engineering challenges • Handle tool calls — Handling errors with is_error • Give Claude custom tools — Handle errors

fields.Front: A coordinator agent in a multi-agent research system delegates one subtopic to a literature search subagent: peer-reviewed studies published since 2024 on four-day school weeks and teacher retention. The query that the subagent sends to an academic index completes normally and matches zero records. Its structured result to the coordinator gives status success, the query that ran, the index that was searched and a result count of 0. The subagents working on the other subtopics have returned their findings without problems, and a synthesis subagent will write the report from what the coordinator passes on. How should the coordinator treat this result? A. Treat the absence of matching studies as a finding, and pass it to synthesis with the query and index that were used. B. Retry the same query against the same index with exponential backoff, and accept a zero count after the third attempt. C. Mark the subtopic as a coverage gap caused by an unavailable source, and state that in the final report's limitations. D. Report that research on the subtopic does not exist, and have synthesis present that as one of the report's findings.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. The query completed and matched nothing: status success with a result count of 0 is a valid empty result, not a failure. It is information, namely that this index holds no matching studies for this query. Option A passes it on as a finding, scoped by the query and the index, so that synthesis can state exactly what was searched. Option B treats a completed query as a failed one; retries suit access failures such as timeouts, and repeating a query that ran correctly returns the same zero after a delay. Option C misreports the cause, because the source was available and answered. Option D accepts the result but stretches it: zero matches for one query in one index do not show that research on the subtopic does not exist. The coordinator may also decide to widen the search, but that is a decision about research scope, not about error recovery. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.3 References: • Give Claude custom tools — Handle errors • Handle tool calls — Handling errors with is_error

fields.Front:
A five-hour audit of a very large codebase is run by a developer productivity system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator agent assigns each of six packages to a subagent. The job runs on shared build machines that are sometimes reclaimed mid-run, which discards everything on the machine's local disk; a shared network volume persists. When that happens, the job restarts from the beginning: the coordinator has no record of which packages were finished, and every subagent repeats its work. The team wants a restarted job to pick up from where the interrupted one stopped.

Which design best achieves this?

A. Wrap each subagent call in retry logic with exponential backoff, so that an interrupted subagent is started over automatically.
B. Have each agent export its state to the shared volume, and have the coordinator load a manifest of those exports when the job restarts.
C. Have the restarted coordinator spawn the same six subagents, and ask each one to report what it had found before the interruption.
D. Have each subagent compact its conversation at regular intervals, so that less of its context is at risk when a machine is reclaimed.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. A reclaimed machine loses its memory and local disk, so a restarted job can continue only from state written somewhere durable before the interruption. Option B is the pattern the exam guide gives for crash recovery: each agent exports structured state to a known location, and on restart the coordinator loads a manifest of those exports, skips the finished packages and injects the saved state into the prompts of agents that have work left. Option A restarts an interrupted subagent from its original prompt, which repeats the work, and does nothing for a coordinator that was itself lost. Option C asks new subagent instances to recall what earlier ones found, but each invocation starts fresh. Option D manages how full a context is and records nothing a restarted coordinator can read. Currency note (Oct 2026): Agent SDK docs also describe resuming a session on another host through a session store or by moving the session file, and call passing captured state into a fresh prompt often more robust. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Work with sessions — Resume across hosts • How we built our multi-agent research system — Production reliability and engineering challenges • Memory tool — Multisession software development pattern

fields.Front:
To add tests to a large legacy codebase, a developer productivity agent built with the Claude Agent SDK works in two phases. In the first, the main agent mapped the repository: where test files live, which fixtures exist and which three modules have no coverage. For the second, it spawns one subagent per uncovered module, so that their verbose file reads stay out of the main agent's context. A trial run shows each subagent spending most of its turns rediscovering the test layout and fixtures, and two of them propose new fixtures that duplicate existing ones.

What should change before the second phase is run for real?

A. Run the second phase in the main agent instead, where the first phase's findings are already present in context.
B. Tell each subagent to begin by repeating the first phase's mapping, so that its picture of the repository is complete.
C. Summarize the first phase's key findings, and include that summary in the prompt that each subagent starts with.
D. Give each subagent a longer turn limit, so that it has time to rediscover the layout before it investigates its module.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Each subagent starts with a fresh context and receives only the prompt it is given, so nothing the main agent learned in the first phase reaches it unless that prompt carries it. Option C summarizes the key findings, the test layout, the existing fixtures and the uncovered modules, and injects them into each subagent's initial context; the subagents can then start on their modules, and the main agent's context remains free of their verbose output. Option A gives up that isolation: the file reads of three investigations would accumulate in the main agent. Options B and D accept the duplicated discovery and pay for it in turns, and neither stops subagents from proposing fixtures that already exist. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs add a fork subagent that inherits the whole conversation; it is off by default in the Agent SDK, and other subagents start fresh. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Subagents in the SDK — What subagents inherit • How we built our multi-agent research system — Appendix • Create custom subagents — Fork the current conversation

fields.Front:
A developer productivity agent built with the Claude Agent SDK has spent a long session exploring an unfamiliar payments codebase, reading dozens of files with Read and Grep. Early in the session it correctly identified the three classes that implement refund handling. Many turns later, asked which class validates a refund amount, it answers that "a validator class typically handles this" and names a class that does not exist; two similar questions get answers that contradict each other. Engineers expect to keep questioning the agent about this codebase for several more hours.

Which practice best counteracts this?

A. Have the agent record key findings in a scratchpad file as it explores, and consult that file when it answers later questions.
B. Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to name specific classes and never to describe what such code typically does.
C. Raise the agent's effort level, so that it reasons for longer before it answers each question about the codebase.
D. Have the agent re-read every file it has opened so far before it answers each new question about the codebase.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Naming a class that does not exist, falling back on what code "typically" does and contradicting itself are the signs of context degradation in an extended session: the specific findings from early exploration are no longer being used reliably. Option A moves those findings out of the conversation into a file that the agent keeps up to date and consults, so later answers rest on recorded facts and not on a long, crowded history. Option B asks for specifics that the degraded context no longer supplies, so it changes the wording of answers more than their accuracy. Option C adds reasoning, not the missing facts. Option D pours every file back into the context before each answer, which worsens the condition causing the problem. Currency note (Oct 2026): Claude Code docs use "scratchpad" for a per-session temporary directory; the guide's scratchpad file means a notes file that the agent keeps and consults. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Effective context engineering for AI agents — Context engineering for long-horizon tasks • Best practices for Claude Code — Manage context aggressively • Explore the .claude directory — Session scratchpad directory

fields.Front:
A structured data extraction system pulls the supplier, total and due date from incoming documents. On a labeled validation set of 10,000 documents it reaches 97% field accuracy overall, above the 95% target, and the operations lead wants to stop human review of every extraction that the model marks as high confidence. The validation set mirrors production volume: about 94% typed invoices, 4% scanned delivery notes and 2% handwritten receipts. Accuracy has only ever been reported as the single overall figure.

What should happen before human review is reduced?

A. Run the validation set several more times, and confirm that the overall figure stays at or above the 95% target.
B. Raise the score that counts as high confidence, and apply the stricter cut-off to all three document types.
C. Remove human review for a trial month, and compare the number of downstream corrections with the month before.
D. Break accuracy down by document type and by field, and confirm that each segment meets the 95% target.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. A single overall figure is dominated by the largest segment. With typed invoices at 94% of the set, they could be at 99% while the other 6% of documents sit near 66%, and the total would come to about 97% (0.94 × 0.99 + 0.06 × 0.66 ≈ 0.97). Option D checks accuracy by document type and by field before any review is removed, which is how to learn whether scanned notes, handwritten receipts or one particular field falls short. Option A repeats the same aggregate; consistency across runs is a useful signal, but it cannot reveal what the average hides. Option B tightens a threshold without knowing whether confidence tracks accuracy in the small segments. Option C would find weak segments by letting their errors reach downstream systems first. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • Define success and build evaluations — Eval design principles • Demystifying evals for AI agents — Maintain and use the eval long-term

fields.Front:
Each document processed by a structured data extraction system receives one confidence score from the model, and documents that score under 0.80 go to a human review queue. The 0.80 threshold was chosen by intuition. An audit against hand-labeled documents finds that documents scoring above 0.90 often contain a wrong tax amount while their other fields are correct, and that most documents in the queue have only one doubtful field. The reviewers cannot keep up with the queue.

Which TWO changes would make the review routing reliable? (Select TWO.)

A. Set each field's review threshold by comparing confidence scores with actual accuracy on a labeled validation set.
B. Have the model output a confidence score for each extracted field, in place of the single score for the whole document.
C. Add a prompt instruction telling the model to report lower confidence whenever it is unsure about a tax amount.
D. Raise the single document threshold from 0.80 to 0.95, so that more of the documents with a wrong tax amount are sent to review.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and B. Two things are wrong with the routing: one score per document cannot show which field is doubtful, and the 0.80 threshold was never checked against actual accuracy. Option B gives a score for each field, so a reviewer's attention goes to the tax amount and not to a whole document. Option A calibrates each field's threshold on labeled data, which is what would reveal that tax amounts need a stricter cut-off than fields that are rarely wrong. Option D keeps the document-level score, remains a guess, and sends far more documents to reviewers who are already behind. Option C asks the model to adjust its own confidence without any measurement; the exam guide treats model confidence as useful for routing only once it has been calibrated against a labeled validation set. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • Demystifying evals for AI agents — Design the eval harness and graders • Define success and build evaluations — Grade your evaluations

fields.Front:
About 20,000 documents a week pass through a structured data extraction system. Its accuracy was validated by document type and by field, and extractions with high model confidence go straight to the accounting system without review. Two reviewers have time to check about 400 of those unreviewed extractions each week. Typed invoices make up 95% of the volume; customs forms and handwritten receipts make up the rest, and new supplier layouts appear every month. The team wants to keep measuring the error rate of the unreviewed extractions and to notice new kinds of error early.

How should the 400 weekly checks be chosen?

A. As a stratified random sample of the high-confidence extractions, with a quota drawn from each document type.
B. As a simple random sample of the high-confidence extractions, with each one given the same chance of selection.
C. As the 400 high-confidence extractions with the lowest confidence scores among those that skipped review.
D. As the same 400 labeled validation documents each week, with the results compared from week to week.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. The team wants two things from 400 checks: a continuing measure of the error rate in extractions that nobody reviews, and early sight of new kinds of error. Option A draws at random within each document type, so the small groups are measured every week instead of being left to chance. Option B is unbiased for the overall rate, but with typed invoices at 95% of volume it would put only about 20 of the 400 checks on customs forms and handwritten receipts combined, too few to measure them or to catch a new failure there. Option C is not random and looks only near the threshold, so it never examines the confident mistakes that are the real exposure. Option D re-tests documents whose answers are already known, and it contains none of the new supplier layouts arriving in production. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • Demystifying evals for AI agents — How evals fit with other methods for a holistic understanding of agents • Define success and build evaluations — Eval design principles

fields.Front:
Briefing reports on listed companies are produced by a multi-agent research system. Its search and analysis subagents return prose summaries to a coordinator agent, which condenses them into one summary for a synthesis subagent; a report subagent then formats every section as bulleted lists. Reviewers raise two complaints: statements in the reports cannot be traced to the documents they came from, and five years of quarterly revenue figures are hard to compare when they are written out as bullets.

Which TWO changes address these complaints? (Select TWO.)

A. Require subagents to return each claim with its source URL and excerpt, and have later agents keep that mapping intact.
B. Have the report subagent append a list of the URLs that the search subagents visited to the end of each report.
C. Have the report subagent present financial figures as tables, while keeping narrative material such as news in prose.
D. Have the report subagent convert the bulleted sections into tables, and apply that one format across the report.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and C. The two complaints have separate causes. Attribution is lost at the two summarization steps: prose summaries, condensed once more by the coordinator, no longer say which document supports which statement. Option A makes each claim travel with its source and excerpt as a structured mapping that later agents preserve, so every statement in a report can be traced. The second complaint is about form: one format is applied to every kind of content. Option C renders each type appropriately, with financial series in tables and narrative in prose. Option B lists where the system looked but does not connect any claim to any source, so nothing becomes traceable. Option D replaces one uniform format with another; tables suit the revenue figures and little else, and it leaves attribution untouched. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6 References: • How we built our multi-agent research system — Appendix • How we built our multi-agent research system — Architecture overview for Research • Reduce hallucinations — Basic hallucination minimization strategies

fields.Front:
A multi-agent research system is compiling a report on remote work. Its document analysis subagent returns each finding as a structured record with three fields: the claim, the source URL and a supporting excerpt. Two records disagree: one says that 31% of employees work remotely at least one day a week, and the other says 44%. The draft written by the system's synthesis subagent states that credible sources contradict each other on this point. When you open the two sources, the first reports a survey carried out in 2021 and the second a survey carried out in 2024.

Which change best prevents this kind of misreading?

A. Tell the synthesis subagent to keep the larger of two differing figures, since newer surveys tend to report higher values.
B. Tell the synthesis subagent to present both figures as a disagreement between sources, each with its source URL.
C. Require the subagents to add the publication or data collection date to every structured finding they return.
D. Tell the synthesis subagent to average two differing figures, and to cite both sources for the combined value.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. The two figures measure the same thing three years apart, but the records carry no date, so the synthesis subagent could not tell a change over time from a contradiction. Option C adds the publication or data collection date to every structured finding, which lets synthesis report a rise from 31% in 2021 to 44% in 2024. Option A guesses which figure is newer from its size, which is not evidence of when it was collected. Option B is the right treatment for a real conflict between figures for the same period, but here it would go on labeling a trend as a disagreement. Option D blends two different years into a number that describes neither. The missing information has to be supplied upstream, where the source is read, and cannot be inferred at synthesis. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6 References: • How we built our multi-agent research system — Prompt engineering and evaluations for research agents • Prompting best practices — Long context prompting

fields.Front:
For a report on remote work, the document analysis subagent of a multi-agent research system returns each finding to the coordinator agent as a structured record with the claim, the source URL, a supporting excerpt and the data collection date. Two records describe the same quarter of 2024: a national statistics office reports that 31% of employees work remotely at least one day a week, and an industry survey with a much larger sample reports 44%. Both sources are credible, and they define remote work differently. At present the analysis subagent forwards only the statistics office figure, reasoning that it is the more official source.

How should the document analysis subagent handle the two figures?

A. Forward only the industry survey figure instead, since a survey with a much larger sample gives the more reliable estimate.
B. Forward both figures with their sources and definitions, marked as conflicting, and leave the coordinator to reconcile them.
C. Forward the midpoint of the two figures as a single value, and cite both of the sources as the origin of that value.
D. Forward neither figure, and note that the rate of remote work could not be established for that quarter of 2024.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Both figures describe the same quarter and both sources are credible, so this is a real conflict, not a difference over time; the differing definitions of remote work may explain it. Option B completes the analysis with both values included and annotated as conflicting, with their sources and definitions, and leaves the reconciliation to the coordinator; the report can then present the point as contested, with attribution. Option A replaces one arbitrary selection with another, since a larger sample does not settle which definition the report should use. Option C manufactures a value that neither source reported and that corresponds to neither definition. Option D discards two credible measurements and reports ignorance where there is evidence. The current behavior fails for the same reason as Option A: the subagent is quietly making a choice that belongs to the coordinator. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.6 References: • How we built our multi-agent research system — Architecture overview for Research • Reduce hallucinations — Basic hallucination minimization strategies
